en: The Essential Explanation of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra:

The Diagram of the Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu, the Universal Fusion and Inexhaustibility of the Objects of Contemplation according to the Teachings on the Proper Timing for the Practice of the Worthy One.
The Bhikṣu Jiehuan of the White Lotus Temple in Wēn-líng, Sòng, has compiled this work.

Previously, Jiehuan found that the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* was as vast and boundless as the ocean-treasury, difficult to investigate exhaustively. He therefore repeatedly studied the commentary and treatises of the Elder Fāngshān.

Having composed a preface on the essential points and categorized the purport of the sūtra, he slightly clarified its outlines. Subsequently, he continued to string together and edit the pure [teachings].

Master Guo Ming compiled the *Xiuzheng Yi* (Rituals for Cultivation and Realization). Regarding his brief explanation of the sacred names and their symbolic significance (*biaofa*), he has frequently received inquiries from the wise and accomplished.

Wishing to exhaust the profundity of the nine assemblies, he has taken the essential outline of National Teacher Qingliang as his basis, collated it with the [original] treatise, and composed this separate commentary.
He takes Fāngshān as the primary authority and Qingliang as an auxiliary support. Having thoroughly investigated the entire Tripiṭaka...

This work consists of eighteen thousand words. It is my hope that readers will find no difference between this being the opening of a great scripture within a single speck of dust, or beholding the entire Dharma-realm in the space of a finger-snap.
Written on the first day of the Lantern Festival in the year Wushen of the Jianyan era.
Initial Preface.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha’s Great Vaipulya* directly reveals the fundamental, true virtues and functions of the Buddha-nature, which is equal for all Buddhas and sentient beings.
It is that which all Buddhas of the three periods of time have equally realized; that which Bodhisattvas of the ten directions have equally cultivated;

that which the assembly of sages throughout the great trichiliocosm have equally revered; and that which all sentient beings within the dharma-realm equally possess. When Śākyamuni Tathāgata first attained [enlightenment]...
The Perfectly Awakened One, wishing to clarify the causes to be cultivated and the fruits to be realized, and desiring that all people might cultivate and realize them together,
manifested the body of a ten-thousand-fathom Vairocana Buddha and preached this teaching for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and Ānanda Sāgara.
It was compiled among the Cakravāḍa mountains and divided into three sections according to the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of beings.
The first section contains verses equal in number to the atoms within thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and chapters equal in number to the atoms within one four-continent world system.
The Middle Section contains four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters;
the Lower Section contains one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters. All were expounded from a single voice, yet each being understood according to their own kind.

For those of superior faculties who hear this, it accords with their nature and pervades all lands—expounded as atoms, expounded as dust motes, blazing forth without interruption—thus [filling] the great trichiliocosm.
Even the atoms of the buddha-fields are insufficient to exhaustively describe it; it is merely designated by means of great numbers.

Those of middling capacity, upon hearing this, understand only the sutras of the present assembly and do not reach the full extent of the discourse on the atoms of the fields; therefore, the verses and chapters are somewhat few. Those of inferior capacity, upon hearing this—
Because the human mind is limited and verbal expression is constrained by fixed measures, only one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters were obtained;
these have been transmitted without being complete. The present sutra consists of forty-five thousand verses and thirty-nine chapters.

Following the initial compilation, it was concealed within the Dragon Palace. Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, exercising his spiritual power, retrieved it from the oceanic treasury and observed that the previous two versions were vast and incomplete.

If the profound ocean were not something the human world could fathom, [the teachings] would have remained recited in the western regions and returned to the Five Indic Kingdoms, rather than being disseminated throughout the Middle Kingdom (China).

Although its vast texts and abundant meanings exhaust the phenomena of the Dharma-realm and reach the limits of the atoms within all lands, they exist solely to illuminate the virtue of one's own inherent nature.
Thus, the Great Vaipulya (Mahāvaipulya) is the substance that is perfectly realized in every single thing; it is merely that [this realization] has been restricted by...

Sentient consciousness is thus bound and made small. The *Avataṃsaka* is inherently possessed by every practitioner, yet because they are mired in worldly toil (*kleśa*), they lose sight of this *Avataṃsaka*.
This sutra reveals the ocean of wisdom without departing from sentient consciousness; it is the wondrous function of the profuse arising of all worldly toils.
When one realizes perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment, this is the practice of the *Avataṃsaka* Buddha—the essence of the Great Vaipulya. It should be understood as such.

When this state manifests before one, it is not obtained from another; faith means that it is inherently possessed by one's own nature. Thus, the essential method for explaining and pointing it out must be investigated.
That which is explained in this sutra takes the Dharmakāya of Vairocana as its essence and the wondrous wisdom of Mañjuśrī as its function.
By relying on wisdom to sever habitual tendencies, the wondrous conduct of Samantabhadra serves as the cause. When habits are exhausted and wisdom is perfected, [the result is attained].
Thus, Maitreya, who is in the stage of succession, serves as the fruition. The essential substance of the One Treasury does not depart from these four;
therefore, Vairocana is taken as the teaching master, which establishes the essence. Mañjuśrī is taken as the foremost of faith, which initiates the function.
The "Practice of Samantabhadra" indicates the cause; it begins with the Ten Faiths and concludes with the Five Ranks, culminating in the vision of Maitreya, which indicates the fruit.
Yet, why must the essence and function, as well as cause and fruit, necessarily rely upon Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya? In Sanskrit, Vairocana means "Universal Radiance."
In the Buddha, it is the pure *dharmakāya*; in humans, it is the wondrous nature of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇajñāna*).
When the *Avataṃsaka* takes this as its essence, it does so precisely because it desires sentient beings to perceive this wondrous nature and thereby realize the *dharmakāya*.
In Sanskrit, Mañjuśrī means "Wondrous Virtue" (*Sudarśana*). In the Buddha, he is the Great Wisdom of Universal Radiance; in humans, he is the mind of wondrous observation.
The *Avataṃsaka* takes this as its function because it seeks directly to cause sentient beings to clarify their wondrous mind and realize great wisdom.
As for Samantabhadra: his virtue is all-pervasive, hence he is called "Universal" (*Samanta*); he protects those above and benefits those below, hence he is called "Worthy" (*Bhadra*).

In the Buddha, he represents true, pure, and wondrous conduct; in ordinary people, he represents the functioning of worldly afflictions and karma. The *Avataṃsaka* takes this as its cause because it seeks directly—
Sentient beings transform their afflictions (*kleśa*) into sublime practices. In Sanskrit, Maitreya means "The Compassionate One" (*Maitrīputra*).
Within the Buddha-dharma, he is the Lord of the Stage of Succession (*kṣetra-parigraha*); among humans, he is one who has attained the body of a "once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*).

That the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* treats this as the fruition is because it directly desires that sentient beings leave behind the state of a once-returner and proceed to the stage of succession. Thus, the essence and function of the *Avataṃsaka*— [Note: The provided text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the content up to that point.]

Regarding cause and effect, Buddhas and sentient beings are one and the same. It is only because Buddhas have harmonized with awakening while sentient beings have harmonized with the dust of sensory objects that there is a distinction between them.

If, through this sutra, one reflects back for even a single thought-moment to extinguish the dust and harmonize with awakening, then transforming from the ordinary state into sainthood is as easy as turning over one's hand.
Thereupon, one’s own Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya will manifest perfectly right where one stands.
This means that at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one attains perfect awakening; this faith is not false.

Second, regarding the explanation of the title: "Mahāvaipulya-buddha" indicates the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* explains the sublime practices. Fundamental wisdom is itself equanimity.
The Buddha-nature is suchness. Wondrous practice is the functional manifestation of the fundamental, true virtue. "Great" refers to the essence reaching its ultimate limit, being all-encompassing;
all beings, from the wriggling insects to the wise and the foolish, possess it. Its terminology is identical to the *dharmadhātu*; it is perfectly square, equal, unchanging, and immovable.
"Vast" refers to the function being equal to the great void; it is pervasive and inclusive, without obstruction or hindrance. The Buddha is primordial wisdom.

The term "fruit" refers to the result; "flower" refers to the causes of the myriad practices. Speaking of flowers in contrast to the fruit, "adornment" means that these causal flowers adorn the resultant Buddha.
When the mind is forgotten and illumination is relinquished, there is neither adornment nor non-adornment.
Only then, when the ten virtues of merit, wisdom, practice, and vows are perfected, does one realize the ten bodies of Vairocana. Qingliang (Zhiyan) said: "Mahāvaipulya..."
The *Dharmas* are that which is realized; the *Buddha-Flower Adornment* (*Buddhāvatamsaka*) is the person who realizes it.

That which is realized does not depart from fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the one who realizes it does not depart from sublime practice (*praṇīta-caryā*). Indeed, these two are of one principle.

The *Sūtra* then penetrates and encompasses the dharmas that are explained, serving as a fixed essence that remains unchanging for ten thousand ages. Regarding the formulation of the title of this scripture, the result is mentioned first and...
Why are both [cause and fruit] presented together? By placing the fruit first and the cause afterward, it is shown that this fruit-Buddha was originally possessed by him;

it is merely through the adornment of the causal flowers that it subsequently becomes manifest. The reason for presenting them together is the desire that cause and fruit may mutually support one another.
For without the fruit, the cause cannot be established; and without the cause, the fruit cannot be accomplished.

It is for this reason that this sutra first cites the fruit to encourage practice, and subsequently details the practice that leads to that fruit. The essence of this entire scripture and its title may be seen therein.
The general outline for the three sections of the forty chapters across the ten assemblies is divided into three parts: the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination.

First, the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Ruler" constitutes the Introduction. Second, from the "Chapter on the Tathāgata’s Manifestation of Signs" onwards constitutes the Main Body. Third, the [Dissemination]...

From the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prakāśana-parivarta*) onwards constitutes the *Pariṇāmanā-vibhāga* (Section on Dissemination). (According to Qingliang, from the passage in the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta": "At that time, Mañjuśrī emerged from the Well-Abiding Pavilion" onwards constitutes the *Pariṇāmanā-vibhāga*).

Among these three categories, each possesses five stages of dharma-gates, designated as the two kinds of eternal paths: the cause and fruit of the Three Circles (*tri-parivarta*). As for the five stages of dharma-gates, they are:
the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), the Ten Transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*), the Ten Grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*), and the Eleventh Ground (*ekādaśa-bhūmi*).
Regarding the three cycles of cause and effect: from the "Worldly Rulers" chapter of the first assembly through the six chapters ending with the *Vairocana* chapter constitutes one cycle.
This represents the Buddha’s own five stages of cause and effect, serving as an exhortation to practice by citing the fruition, specifically the section on the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
From the second assembly through the eighth assembly, from the "Names of the Buddhas" chapter to the thirty-two chapters ending with the "Appearance of the Tathāgata," constitutes [the second cycle].

One cycle. This constitutes the causal and resultant stages of the five positions for those who advance in practice; it is established as the section on the Dharma-treatment for training, cultivation, realization, and fruition.

(The ninth assembly, the "Chapter on Transcending the World," clarifies the constant path of benefiting sentient beings after the realization of the fruit, and is thus generally included within the section on the Dharma-treatment for training, cultivation, realization, and fruition.

The tenth assembly, the "Dharmadhātu Chapter," marks the completion of Sudhana’s southern journey from beginning to end as one cycle; this fully manifests and reiterates the causal and resultant stages of the five positions, serving as the means for departure.

Regarding the section on "The Manifestation of the Dharma-realm through Words, Reliance, and Practice," there are two kinds of eternal paths: first, the eternal path of benefiting sentient beings while remaining unstained by worldly conditions, as found in the "Chapter on Leaving the World";
second, the eternal path of the Buddha-fruit where cultivation is forgotten and realization is transcended, as found in the "Chapter on the Dharma-realm."

This is the general outline of this collection. (Qingliang [Xuanzhuang] divides it as follows: the first assembly’s six chapters constitute the "Section on Exalting the Fruit and Encouraging Joyful Faith";

the second through seventh assemblies’ thirty-one chapters constitute the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generating Understanding, Separating from the World"; and the single chapter on the Dharma-realm constitutes the "Section on Entrusting the Teaching, Advancing in Practice, and Accomplishing Virtue. He comprehensively judges the entirety of this collection by means of the four terms: faith, understanding, practice, and realization.
Regarding the statement that there are ten assemblies and forty chapters in this scripture: since this scripture is said to symbolize the Dharma, there are ten locations.

There are ten assemblies, which expound the dharmas of cultivation and realization such as the Ten Faiths and the Ten Grounds. In each assembly, the tenfold congregations are assigned to the ten *pāramitās*.
The reason each is said to be "ten" is that ten is a perfect number, thereby perfectly manifesting the sudden teaching (*tun-fa*). The first assembly at the Bodhimanda consists of six chapters;
the second assembly in the Hall of Universal Radiance consists of six chapters; and the third assembly in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven consists of six chapters.
The fourth assembly was at the Yāma Heaven in four chapters; the fifth assembly was at Tuṣita Heaven in three chapters; the sixth assembly was at Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven in one chapter;
the seventh assembly was at the Third Dhyāna Heaven in one chapter; the eighth assembly was at the Hall of Universal Radiance in eleven chapters;

the ninth assembly was at the Hall of Universal Radiance in one chapter; and the tenth assembly was at Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park in one chapter. These constitute the ten assemblies across ten locations. Part Four.

There are ten chapters. Some speak of "seven locations and nine assemblies," which results from dividing the three assemblies at the Universal Radiance Hall into two locations and omitting the section on the third dhyāna heaven, thereby reducing one location and one assembly.

Nevertheless, although there are ten locations and ten assemblies, they do not depart from the teaching of a single location and a single assembly—the Palace of Universal Radiance of Great Wisdom and the Metropolis of the Flower Treasury of the Dharma Realm. It is merely according to the progression [of the teaching].
The manifestation of the stages of practice is a symbolic representation of the Dharma; it does not possess the characteristics of coming and going as perceived by ordinary sentient beings.
Therefore, the sutra repeatedly states: "At that time, the World-Honored One, without departing from the Bodhimanda or the Hall of Universal Radiance, ascended to such-and-such a place."
Regarding the three cycles of cause and effect: the first cycle concerns the exhortation to practice the causes and effects of the five stages of the Buddha’s own career.

In the first assembly at the Bodhimaṇḍa, six chapters of the Dharma were taught to reveal the Buddha’s own deeds—cultivating causes over vast eons to adorn the ocean of lands and benefit sentient beings—in order to encourage future students. By causing them to see these actual traces, they are inspired to advance in their cultivation.
Furthermore, Qingliang’s topical outline designates this as the "Section on Citing the Fruit to Encourage Joy and Inspire Faith. Its intent is the same [as the previous]. It consists of:

First, the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World Lord"; Second, the "Chapter on the Manifestation of Signs by the Tathāgata"; Third, the "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra"; Fourth, the "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the World";
Fifth, the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World"; and Sixth, the "Chapter on Vairocana."
The first chapter, "The Exquisite Adornment of the World Lord," is the general introduction that initiates the ten assemblies.
Regarding the Bodhisattvas at the Flower Adornment Assembly, this particular assembly is taught at the site of the Bodhimanda to clarify the matters of cultivation and realization over vast eons;
therefore, it is taught at the location of the Bodhimanda. Since only the practice of Samantabhadra can lead to entry into realization, it relies upon Samantabhadra.
"Sā" means to initiate. "Shen Tian" (Divine Beings) are all titled "World Lords," meaning they preside over and protect the world through their merit and spiritual power.
Within the assembly of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are generally forty-one groups.

At the initial gathering of the Dharma assembly, each group offered verses of praise to manifest the five stages of the Dharma-gates cultivated by the Tathāgata during his causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*). Each of these ocean-like assemblies possessed majestic virtue and blazing splendor.
The ten bodies of Vairocana are perfectly interfused and brilliantly manifest, together adorning the Dharma assembly; therefore, this is named the "Chapter on Wondrous Adornment" (Miaoyan-pin).
At the beginning of this chapter, it speaks of the site of enlightenment where perfect awakening was attained—the Bodhimanda—and the lion throne adorned with various jewels.

Within these objective realms and images, they mutually reflect one another: the Buddha occupies the precious throne and attains supreme perfect enlightenment; his wisdom penetrates the three periods of time, and his body pervades the ten directions.

For example, just as empty space contains all images within it, this generally clarifies that the resultant awakening possesses boundless virtues and functions, both in its primary and secondary aspects (the environment and its inhabitants).

Next, the gathering of the assembly is described, consisting of forty-one groups; these represent the causes and effects of the five stages of the Buddha’s own person, serving as the fundamental basis for further cultivation.
First, the ten bodhisattvas beginning with Samantabhadra constitute one assembly, representing the dharma of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Next, the ten bodhisattvas beginning with Sāgaraprabha, together with the assemblies of the Vajradhara spirits, the Kramagamana spirits, the Maṇḍala spirits, the Nagara spirits, the Pṛthivī spirits, the Parvata spirits, the Vana spirits, and the Oṣadhi spirits, constitute ten assemblies, representing the dharma of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*). Furthermore, next...
The ten assemblies, from the Lord of Crops to the Lord of Day, represent the ten *dharmas* of practice (*caryā*).
Next, the ten assemblies, from the *asura*s to the Sun Deity (*Sūryadeva*), represent the ten *dharmas* of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Next, the ten assemblies, from the Heaven of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) to Maheśvara, represent the ten *bhūmi*s. Once these assemblies have gathered, each is able to preach the Dharma and praise the clarity of the Tathāgata.
The five stages of Dharma practice cultivated herein serve as the foundation for all subsequent methods of advancement;
therefore, they constitute the fundamental school of progressive cultivation.
First, representing the assembly of those in the stage of the Ten Faiths, there are Bodhisattvas Samantabhadra, numbering as many as the atoms within ten Buddha-fields, who stand at the head.
The "Head" (Shou) represents the inexhaustible conduct of Samantabhadra. The ten names share the same title, "Universal" (Pu), which represents the perfectly integrated conduct of Samantabhadra.
The character "Universal" itself clarifies his own practice; these are all the shared path of all Buddhas.
Using this to represent the Ten Faiths demonstrates that the shared path of all Buddhas arises from faith based upon the great conduct of Samantabhadra.
This is the initial foundation for entering the Dharma.
Next, it symbolizes the assembly of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). The first ten bodhisattvas with distinct names, such as Sāgaraprabha and others, symbolize the fruit-practices of the ten stages.
The reason for citing these ten distinct names following the ten "Universals" (*samanta*) is to symbolize that [the practices] arise based upon the conduct of Samantabhadra.
This represents the practice of differentiation. Next, from the Vajrapāṇi spirits to the Nine Classes of Spirits headed by Bhaiṣajyarāja, these represent the causal practices of the Ten Abodes.
Each of these assemblies consists of as many beings as there are atoms in a buddha-field, all of which symbolize the perfectly integrated practice of their respective stages.
The Vajrapāṇi deities represent the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) protecting the Dharma and guarding the truth without being corrupted.

The Body-attendant deities represent serving immeasurable Buddhas with immeasurable bodies. The Footstep-following deities represent the fulfillment of all practices in accordance with the Right Path.

The Maṇḍala-ground deities represent the adornment of great vows and the extensive promotion of offerings. The City-guardian deities represent skillfully guarding the city of the mind and adorning it.
Purifying the Buddha-lands: the Earth-Ruling Spirit represents the fulfillment of profound and weighty vows for the sake of all sentient beings;

the Mountain-Ruling Spirit represents the accumulation of roots of goodness that transcend the world with sublime excellence; the Forest-Ruling Spirit represents the trunk of wisdom and the flowers of conduct, providing vast shade through the preaching of the Dharma;

the Medicine-Ruling Spirit represents knowing the faculties [of beings] and skillfully saving them by means of the medicine of the Dharma. This concludes the section on the assembly of the fruits of the Ten Abodes, beginning with...
The "Great Radiance of Ocean Moonlight" symbolizes the capacity for universal inclusion and salvation, the removal of afflictions, and the opening of awakening;

it culminates in the "Radiance of Great Merit and Wisdom," symbolizing that enlightened conduct is sufficient to achieve the realization of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). These are all practices that perfect virtue.

Regarding their retinues: they begin with Vajrapāṇi, symbolizing the maintenance of correctness and indestructibility, and end with Bhaiṣajyarāja, symbolizing the knowledge of the faculties (*indriya*) and skillful means.
"Salvation" refers to the practice of ascending progress. The "Spirit" manifests the penetration of wisdom, responding to the myriad phenomena without deliberate action.

By means of this penetrating wisdom, one relies upon the dwelling place of the Buddha; beginning with the maintenance of rectitude and culminating in skillful salvation, one advances mysteriously along this path through non-thought and non-action.
Thus, one achieves the great fruit of merit known as the "Ocean Moon. This is the first stage of the Ten Abidings.

Regarding the "Abiding in the Generation of the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*), the fact that it is first represented by the assembly of fruits indicates that at the very moment of the initial generation of the mind, one attains perfect enlightenment.
The remaining assemblies represent the names of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) in their proper sequence, and they likewise represent the ten *pāramitās* in their proper sequence.

This is detailed extensively in the treatise. Furthermore, each assembly contains ten names, representing that each single *pāramitā* is itself endowed with ten aspects, thus manifesting their perfect interpenetration and fusion.
Their mutual inclusion is layered and inexhaustible; this is the wondrous function of the single nature and the fundamental substance of all phenomena.
Within what is identical, there are further distinct names because practice varies according to the stage, and thus the symbolic dharmas also vary.
The intent lies in perfect integration and broad comprehension; if one stagnates in a single dharma, then practice will not be comprehensive and wisdom will not increase in clarity. There is none...
Because they have perfected inexhaustible practices, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished as the fruit of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

From the Vajradhara deity down to the hosts of nāgas, devas, and spirits, all are manifestations of the Bodhisattva according to his responsive capacity; the various beings who scatter flowers are not actual ghosts or spirits.
Next is the representation of the assembly of the ten practices. First, the Lord of Crops represents the accomplishment of sentient beings through the dharma of provisions (*sambhāra*).

The Lord of Rivers represents the universal purification and benefit of sentient beings through swift currents. The Lord of Seas represents the capacity to encompass both good and evil, bringing them all into the flow of the Dharma.
The Lord of Waters represents the moistening and benefiting of things according to their needs, capable of purifying all defilements. The Lord of Fire... [text continues]

The Spirit of Divine Manifestation represents the radiance that arises in accordance with conditions to destroy the obscurations of darkness. The Spirit of Wind represents the dispersal and extinction of egoism through the wisdom of equality.
The Spirit of Space represents the vast, brilliant purity and non-attachment of the myriad practices.

The Spirit of the Directions represents the perfect illumination of the ten directions and the great trichiliocosm by means of wisdom. The Spirit of Night represents the illumination of the long cycle of birth and death by means of wisdom.

At night, the Lord of Day deities represent the single mind that is never indolent, illuminating the Sun of the Buddha. Next, the ten groups of deities presiding over the harvest represent the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).
This demonstrates the cause and effect of arising from abiding [in the stages] to initiate practice for the benefit of sentient beings.

Previously, the Bodhisattvas represented the fruit and the deities represented the cause; here, using deities to represent both the beginning and the end indicates that the dharma of the ten practices is itself [the fruit].

The cause is itself the fruit; this constitutes the stage of the provisions for the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). This is because the ten practices of the Buddha-fruit serve as provisions for great-minded sentient beings to advance toward the state of Buddhahood, and they serve as provisions for Bodhisattvas on the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) to nurture their Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*); this is precisely the meaning of cause and fruit mutually supporting one another.
In the teaching of the Three Vehicles, faith, abiding, practice, and orientation are designated as the four kinds of provisions prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), while from the first stage onward—

In the aforementioned [system], the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is distinct; this sutra is not so. From the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) up to the initial mind of the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), these are collectively the Path of Seeing.

The stages of Abiding, Progressing, and Entering (*vihāra-gati-praveśa*) are collectively the preparatory stage (*prayoga*). All three together constitute the Requisites (*sambhāra*). These three advance together and mutually stimulate one another;
to omit any one of them would entail falling into the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), as it is not the Perfect and Sudden Dharma (*yuan-dun fa*). One must directly take the fruit as the basis.

The cause is adorned by the cause so as to adorn the fruit, thereby becoming the Flower Adornment of Buddhahood (*Buddhāvataṃsaka*). The meanings symbolized by its ten assemblies are all practices for benefiting sentient beings.

Their sequence represents the names of the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), and their sequence also represents the Ten Perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) as well as the distinct practices according to their respective stages.
Their perfect interfusion and mutual inclusion are exactly as explained previously; the subsequent sections should also follow this principle. This is because the Ten Perfections...
The five stages of honey represent the universal cultivation [of all practices]; the myriad deeds of a Bodhisattva do not depart from these.

Next, they symbolize the assembly of the ten transferences. First is the asura assembly, which symbolizes dwelling within the ocean of birth and death while harmonizing the ultimate and the conventional truths.
The host of *garuḍas* symbolizes the use of great skillful means to rescue and deliver sentient beings.

The host of *kiṃnaras* symbolizes the mastery of acting in concert with neither the noble nor the mundane. The host of *mahoragas* symbolizes the protection of the monastery and the severing of the net of ignorance.
The host of *yakṣas* symbolizes the protection and rescue of sentient beings living in suffering. The host of devas and *nāgas* symbolizes the arousal [of the Dharma].
The Dharma-cloud rain provides shelter and moistens all; the host of kumbhāṇḍas represents entering the various realms of existence to bestow compassion and benefit sentient beings;
the host of gandharvas represents relying on the fragrance of the five aggregates to bring joy to sentient beings;

the host of the Moon Devas represents cooling the heat of affliction and manifesting precious radiance; and the host of the Sun Devas represents abiding in the heights to benefit those below by illuminating all things.
Success. Regarding the ten assemblies from the Asuras to the Sun Deity representing the Ten Directions:

whereas the previous stages of the Ten Abodes and Ten Practices involved only the cultivation of supramundane compassion and wisdom (*karuṇā* and *prajñā*) and had not yet exhausted engagement in worldly beneficial conduct, this stage involves turning back from the true toward the conventional and turning back from wisdom toward compassion, thereby effecting the perfect integration of the true and the conventional and the non-duality of wisdom and compassion. [One remains] within the ocean of birth and death...
He is like a king: the higher his station, the more humble his conduct. Thus, he is first represented by the King of Asuras and finally by the Sun Deity;
all other [representations] follow his conduct according to his station.
Next, regarding the second section on the assembly of the Dharma of the Ten Stages, first, concerning the five heavens of the desire realm, there are five [sections].
Regarding the first three, the thirteen celestial kings offer praise, saying: "Those who initiate vast karmic activities for the world. The Sūtra’s eulogy of their virtues states:
"All diligently initiate vast activities for all worlds. These celestial kings are none other than Śakra; they dwell in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Possessing great meritorious karma, they dwell in pure abodes with few desires, causing the world to aspire toward them and practice virtuous deeds together;
this is called initiating vast karma. The *Yāma-deva-praśaṃsā-sūtra* states: "They cultivate great roots of goodness, and their minds are always fully endowed [with virtue].
The commentary states: "The fact that this heaven is perpetually bright day and night symbolizes great wisdom. Its possession of manifold virtues and sublime bliss symbolizes..."
This is the joy of the Dharma. Third, the praise of the Tuṣita Heaven: the Sūtra says, "Diligently uphold the names of all Buddhas";
the Śāstra says, "Possessing precepts, concentration, and wisdom, one is born in this heaven. Fourth, the praise of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven:

The *Nirmitadeva-stava* (Hymn of the Emanated Devas). The Sūtra says: "All diligently cultivate the vast Dharma-gates of sovereign skillful means. The Śāstra says:

"This signifies that the Bodhisattva delights in transforming others for his own sake. Next, the five heavens of the Form Realm (rūpadhātu), beginning with the Great Brahmā Heaven (*Mahābrahmā*) of the First Dhyāna, offer praise.
The Sūtra says: "Out of compassion for sentient beings, he radiates light everywhere, causing them to attain happiness. The Śāstra says: "He is free from desire."
"Purity" is the name for Brahmā. It is praised by the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Second Dhyāna. The *Śāstra* states: "These gods have already extinguished sorrow and suffering;

when they speak, light is produced from their mouths, signifying that their teaching illuminates and transforms all universally. It is praised by the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven of the Third Dhyāna. The *Śāstra* states:

"They are already free from sorrow and suffering, possessing only the joy of dhyāna. It is praised by the Bṛhatphala Heaven of the Fourth Dhyāna. The *Sūtra* says: "By means of the dharma of tranquility..."
It serves as a palace. The *Śāstra* states: "Vast merit constitutes the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*); it is praised by Maheśvara at the summit of the Form Realm (*Rūpadhātu*).
The *Sūtra* states: "All diligently observe the signless (*animitta*) dharma; their conduct is impartial. The *Śāstra* states:

As for why there are no assemblies of formless realm devas (*ārūpya-deva*) in this assembly of the *Saddharma-puṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is because those heavens lack the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and are thus invisible. Collectively, those gathered—the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas—are designated as the Four Noble Ones;

these are the śrāvakas who were manifestations at the Dharma-realm assembly, as well as the bhikṣus and spiritual friends. The six realms of existence—gods, humans, asuras, animals, hungry ghosts, and hell-beings—are designated as the Six Ordinary Beings;
these are the deities and spirits of the eight classes who gathered like clouds, as well as the laypeople and spiritual friends. Thus, all the assemblies arrived.
In the *Saṃnipāta*, even yakṣas, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, ghosts, and animals each preached this Dharma-gate;
from this, it is sufficient to know that these are all the provisional manifestations of the Three Bodies and Four Wisdoms of the Sage.

When the assembly of the Dharma had gathered, from among all the ornaments adorning the seat upon which the Tathāgata sat, there emerged bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of Buddha-fields, with Sāgarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña-rāja as their leader.

Each offered worship and spoke verses in praise of the Buddha, thereby clarifying the sameness of the Way throughout antiquity and the present, and extolling the gathering of the assembly of the Dharma. Furthermore—

This serves as the cause for manifesting signs and preaching the Dharma. Because the Buddha, in response to their praise and request, emitted light from between his eyebrows and manifested various sublime signs to preach the Dharma to the assembly, there follows the "Chapter on the Tathāgata Manifesting Signs.
In the preceding section, the assembly represented the dharmas of the five stages up to the tenth bhūmi; however, there was no assembly yet representing the eleventh bhūmi. Now...
I have presumed that since this assembly shares the same path as all Buddhas, it is appropriate to represent the dharmas of the fruit-positions of the eleven stages (*ekādaśabhūmi*).

Those matters not urgently requiring representation have been omitted. In cases where the scripture does not specify the names of the sages, I have supplemented them according to their respective ranks and positions.
Conversely, where many titles are extensively listed but the dharma they represent is singular, I have omitted those instances that could not be fully recorded.
Therefore, I have condensed it. My intention is that the text be concise and the meaning clear, so that those who chant the liturgy may easily admire it without becoming weary or bored.
Furthermore, in this present exposition, I likewise rely on the *Abhidharma-śāstra* to extract essential meanings and present the broad outlines.

Where the original text’s intent was obscure, I have drawn from other volumes to provide simultaneous clarification; where previous expositions were too brief, I have gathered what I have heard to establish the explanation.
[The commentary] is extensive. In some instances, it follows the original phrasing and intent while making slight modifications;
in all cases, it strives for clarity and precision, so that those who study and savor it may easily attain deep understanding without obstruction.
The above concludes the introductory section of the "World Rulers' Sublime Array" chapter (this chapter comprises five fascicles).

The second chapter, "The Tathāgata Manifesting Signs," marks the beginning of the main body of the teaching (*samyak-artha*). Once these bodhisattvas, divine beings, and world-protectors had assembled, they remained silent while requesting the Dharma with thirty-seven questions.
The first question concerned the eighteen kinds of Buddha-dharmas, and the subsequent questions concerned the nineteen kinds of bodhisattva-oceans;
all of these pertain to the spheres of wisdom, conduct, and the qualities and functions of the Buddhas, and serve to initiate this [teaching].
The *Sarvadharma-mukha-sūtra*. The sūtra states: At that time, all the bodhisattvas and the lords of the world had this thought:
"What is this ocean of wisdom? Thereupon, the Tathāgata emitted light and manifested signs to answer their inquiry.
First was the general response, followed by the detailed response, which subsequently formed a sūtra of forty chapters. This is the initial general response.
There are two [types of objects]: first, the object of manifest wisdom, which is this present chapter; second, the object of active manifestation, which is the subsequent chapter.
In this chapter, from between the many teeth of his face, the Buddha emits ten kinds of light that universally illuminate the ten directions through the power of the Buddha’s spiritual authority.
That light was able to recite verses, summoning the ocean-like assemblies of Bodhisattvas from throughout the world-systems to gather together and listen to the Dharma.
Within each and every pore of those Bodhisattva assemblies, various kinds of radiance were manifested;

within each ray of light, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field appeared, universally serving Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field and universally delivering sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field. This is the manifestation of the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma.
It is the characteristic of the sovereign mastery of the elements, essence, nature, wisdom, and compassion—unimpeded and inexhaustible.

The Tathāgata again emitted light from the hair-treasure between his eyebrows, and within that hair-treasure, a multitude of bodhisattvas appeared, each reciting verses of praise to manifest the power of the Tathāgata’s boundless realm and supernormal faculties.
The sutra says: "At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause all bodhisattvas..."
Because the Tathāgata had attained the spiritual power of boundless realms, he emitted light from between his brows that illuminated the ten directions.

Within every single atom, he manifested countless Buddhas. Furthermore, a Bodhisattva named Dharmajayaśabda and others, accompanied by as many Bodhisattvas as there are atoms in an ocean of worlds, emerged simultaneously and spoke verses in praise of the Buddha. This is the manifestation of the ocean of lands.
The obstructing dharmas are the characteristics of the sphere of manifest knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*). This provides a general answer to the preceding question;
therefore, it is called the "Chapter on Manifest Characteristics" (this chapter consists of one fascicle).

The third chapter, "The Samādhi of Samantabhadra," provides a comprehensive response to the preceding questions regarding the manifestation of the objective realm. The virtues of Samantabhadra are all-pervasive, symbolizing the gateway to the Buddha’s practices.
*Samādhi* here is translated as "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*), which refers to the empowerment bestowed upon Samantabhadra by the Buddha’s spiritual power.
This causes them to enter right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), which is the manifestation of the objective realm. As the Sūtra says:
"At that time, Samantabhadra, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, entered the Samādhi of the Body of the All-Pervading Vairocana Treasury.

He was able to manifest all manner of signs within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), give rise to all dharmas of samādhi, and accomplish the ocean of merits of all Buddhas. At that moment, throughout the ten directions of the Dharma-realm..."
Within a single atom there are Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field.

Before each of these Buddhas, Samantabhadra enters this samādhi, thereby enabling all the bodhisattvas to individually attain samādhi-practices and gateways as numerous as atoms. This is the realm of manifest practice.

This serves as a comprehensive answer to the preceding question; hence it is called the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Samādhi. Thus, the explanation of the preceding realms of wisdom and practice is concluded.
From this point onward, the entire collection of dharma-gates consists of nothing other than the integration of all causes and effects within wise practice.

Therefore, the two preceding gates provide a general response; that is to say, the dharmas ranging from the realm of the Buddhas to the bodhisattvas’ setting forth in practice are all fully contained herein.
The subsequent thirty-seven factors of enlightenment constitute the specific response.
The "Chapter on the Accomplishment of the Four Worlds" specifically answers the questions concerning the ocean of worlds and the ocean of sentient beings.

Its intent is to clarify that the myriad differences in the forms of the worlds of sentient beings and Buddhas—the distinctions between suffering and happiness, purity and impurity, and their various transformations—are each accomplished through the power of the karma of one's own practice. Thus, the Sūtra says: "In the oceans of worlds, there are atoms..."
The distinctions of numerical transformations are as follows: when sentient beings who are defiled abide [in this state], it constitutes a transformation of defilement;
when sentient beings who have resolved upon bodhicitta abide [in this state], it constitutes a transformation of purity;

up to the point where that which is accumulated by Bodhisattvas constitutes a transformation of great adornment; and the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas constitutes a transformation of adorned cessation. This is why...
The purpose of saying this is to cause sentient beings to know that the characteristics of defiled and pure objects, as well as suffering and pleasure, all arise from karma;
thereby they will give rise to a correct mind and cultivate the path of transcendence, entering the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom and the ocean of the Buddha’s Flower Treasury.
For this reason, the "Chapter on the Formation of the World" is explained first, followed by the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World.
The "Chapter on Formation" specifically answers the initial arising [of the world] (this chapter and the preceding "Chapter on Samādhi of Samantabhadra" together constitute one fascicle).
The "Chapter on the Five Flower Treasury Worlds" specifically answers the questions concerning the ocean of Buddhas and the ocean of *pāramitās*.
This chapter describes the wondrously adorned realm of the inexhaustible *dharmadhātu* of Vairocana.

It is the retributive fruit realized through practicing the five stages and ten *pāramitās*, based upon the wisdom-essence of the *dharmakāya* and the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra. This is what is called the ocean of Buddhas and the ocean of *pāramitās*.

The Ocean of Honey. A sutra states: This Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean rests upon ten layers of wind-wheels, within a great lotus flower called the Fragrant Banner of the Calyx of the Fragrant Water-Ocean.

Within it, world-systems as numerous as the atoms in countless water-oceans dwell in mutual dependence, and this is termed the "World-Network. At its center is one world-system containing twenty layers.
This Sahā world-system is located in the thirteenth layer; it is the dwelling place of Vairocana Tathāgata.
It is surrounded by ten world-systems, and beyond those ten, there are further one hundred world-systems encircling it, all enclosed by the Great Diamond Rim-Mount (Vajramahācakravāḍa-parvata).
Calculated thus, there are one hundred and eleven world-systems, each of which has its own symbolic significance.

Furthermore, the ten layers of wind-wheels supporting the fragrant water-ocean and producing great lotus flowers as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field signify that the wind-wheel of the Great Vow supports the ocean of Great Wisdom, giving birth to the flowers of boundless sublime practices.
These adorn and sustain the body and the field as the Buddha’s pure land. The single world-system at the center represents the Buddha-stage, which universally encompasses all things.
Pervading all, it serves as the foundation of the myriad dharmas. Next, the ten signify the single cause and single fruit of the five stages.
Furthermore, the hundred signify that within each of the five stages, both cause and fruit possess the ten pāramitās.
Within these, the eleven world-systems each have twenty layers, signifying the ten causes and ten fruits of the progressive advancement through the five stages and the Buddha-stage respectively.
This refers to the fruit. In each and every world-system, there are Buddhas as numerous as atoms; all of them were personally served by Vairocana Tathāgata in the past.
By citing one Buddha from each world-system, each represents the fruit of advancement to its respective stage.
Within each of the hundred world-systems, including the outermost world-system, there are four layers, each containing four Buddhas, representing the four [dhyānas].

Regarding the "Inclusion of Dharmas" (*dharmasaṃgraha*): this clarifies that the ten perfections and myriad practices are supported by the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)—beneficial conduct, kind speech, and shared purpose—as external protections.

Each net of worlds within this realm possesses all manner of supreme and wondrous adornments; these are all the result of the pervasive and universal transformative influence of the Buddha’s wisdom and practice.
Among them, there are also worlds characterized by defilement, which symbolize the Buddha’s compassionate inclusion and transformation of beings.
One does not abandon this. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Defilement and purity both arise through the power of karma; these are what Bodhisattvas transform.

Regarding the term "world-system" (*lokadhātu-jāta*) and "ocean of worlds" (*lokadhātu-samudra*): "system" (*jāta*) refers to the multiplicity of births, while "ocean" (*samudra*) refers to the multiplicity of what is encompassed.
From three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems up to those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one such unit constitutes a single world-system. [The number of] Ganges sands...
A single world-system consists of one world-element; a world-ocean consists of as many world-elements as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
All of these are contained within the great lotus flower named Kūṭāgāra-gandha-ketu; therefore, it is called the Flower Treasury World (*Kusumatalagarbha-lokadhātu*).

The treatise states that from the calculation of thousands of worlds up to the number of grains of sand in the Ganges constitutes a single world-ocean, and that the nature of world-elements numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges constitutes a single world-lineage (*lokadhātu-jāti*). This is precisely [the meaning].
These seed-spheres (*jāti*) are able to encompass oceans [of worlds]. Yet the Sūtra states: "Within the ocean of world-systems (*lokadhātusāgara*), there are seed-spheres of worlds.

According to this scriptural teaching, these are all the results of Vairocana Tathāgata’s past personal service to various Buddhas, manifesting the fruit of his advancement through successive stages. (This chapter comprises three fascicles.)
The sixth chapter, "Vairocana," clarifies that the ancient Vairocana Tathāgata also resided in the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*) to preach the Dharma and benefit sentient beings.

His assembly and dharma-gates were no different from those of the present; it is only that the Buddha’s name differs, as this is due to differences in accordance with the capacities of beings, not because the Buddhas themselves differ.
This follows from the preceding five chapters, which presented the causes and conditions for the present Vairocana’s attainment of enlightenment.

Regarding the matter of benefiting sentient beings, this passage cites the past to corroborate the present, clarifying that the Way is identical throughout the three periods of time and that cause and effect do not differ.

It is intended to enable future practitioners to likewise realize this fruit; therefore, this chapter is further expounded. Together with what preceded it, this serves as an exhortation to practice by pointing toward the fruit within the section on the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
For it is difficult to progress in cultivation without having seen the essence of the Path; thus, this follows immediately after.
Thereafter, he demonstrates the section on practicing the path through the establishment of the Dharma.

In this chapter, it is recounted that in the past, across kalpas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field, there appeared a succession of Buddhas. Among them was a prince named Mahātejaḥprabha, who served these various Buddhas throughout his life.
It is said that [the Buddha] realized all dharma-gates, all beneficial practices, and all samādhis; yet, while four Buddhas are mentioned in alternation, there is no concluding summary.

This is likely because the text of this chapter has not been fully preserved. Qingliang [Weizhong] identifies Great Radiant Light as the previous incarnation of Vairocana, though this is not stated in the sutra.
Furthermore, it is said that these six chapters of the sutra are intended to exhort by citing the fruition.
The Section on the Arising of Joyful Faith (this fascicle comprises one scroll).
The first six chapters, spoken at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), together total eleven scrolls. These clarify the Tathāgata’s reliance upon the gates of the True Dharma.
This concludes the explanation of the first of the three cycles (*trivartman*).
The second cycle consists of the second through the eighth assemblies. Regarding the causes and effects of the five stages for those who advance in practice:
this correctly demonstrates the practitioner’s conduct of progressing through the five stages. First, relying on faith, one brings forth correct wisdom to illuminate and destroy ignorance.
Next, relying on the five stages, one refines the afflictions and habitual tendencies to perfect the ultimate fruit. This is called the "Dharma of Provisioning."

The stages of practice, cultivation, and realization comprise thirty-two categories in total: first, six categories for the stage of the ten faiths; second, six categories for the stage of the ten abidings;
third, four categories for the stage of the ten practices; fourth, three categories for the stage of the ten transferences;
fifth, one category for the stage of the ten bhūmis; sixth, one category for the eleventh bhūmi; and seventh, eleven categories for the stage of the Buddha-fruit.
The *Qingliang ke* (Chengguan’s Commentary) is titled "The Section on Cultivating the Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding.

This means that by cultivating the perfect causes of the five stages, one accords with the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment, thereby enabling sentient beings to skillfully understand the characteristics of cause and effect.
The reason all five stages are said to be "ten" is that each advances by means of ten dharmas.

These five stages—namely, the stage of abiding (*sva-vihāra*), practice (*caryā*), direction (*mukha*), ground (*bhūmi*), and the eleventh ground (*ekādaśabhūmi*)—take the stage of faith (*śraddhā*) as the cause and the [final] stage as the fruit.

This is called the "Dharma-realm practice-gate" in which the causes and fruits of the five stages are perfectly encompassed. Thus, including the initial faith and the final fruit along with the five intermediate stages, there are seven.

As for the specific mention of the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*): faith is the fundamental essence of the fruit; because it is perfectly pervasive from beginning to end, no gradations are established, and thus it is not counted among them.
Emerging from within faith and moving toward the fruit, the stages involve progressive advancement; therefore, numbers are employed to clarify them.
Faith is like a seed, the stages are like its sprouting, and the fruit is like the ripening of the grain. At the moment of sprouting, there is the husk.

This is the preface to the *Chaiyehua* (Unfolding the Flower). Although the seeds and fruits are inherently indivisible within their totality, the Way is fundamentally without number, which corresponds to faith and the fruit.
The Dharma, however, possesses number, which refers to the five stages (*pañca-vasthā*).

Yet, the stages are limited to five because the celestial numbers are five, the terrestrial numbers are five, and the numbers of the myriad dharmas are likewise five; thus, the celestial pattern is established.

There are five planets; the earth has five latitudinal peaks (the Five Sacred Mountains); human conduct consists of the five constant virtues; internally there are the five viscera, and externally there are the five limbs.

Even the confluences at the chest are precisely five. Expanding and extending this further, there are the five directions, five colors, five elements, and five musical notes—so numerous that they cannot all be enumerated.
Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra establishes positions based on the number five, for it embodies the nature of all phenomena.
This is the natural order of things. Regarding the fact that the Dharma-gate of the five positions takes faith as its primary cause:

it is intended for those practicing the *Avataṃsaka* to externally believe that the dharmas of the five positions are all the virtuous functions of their own mind, and internally to believe that the Buddha of one's own mind is identical in essence with Vairocana.
Only when the mind and the Dharma correspond can one advance in cultivation; thus, wisdom and practice will not be deluded. Upon reaching [this stage]...
The fruit ultimately does not depart from the dharma of initial faith. It is like a seed that first possesses its entire form before it sprouts;
when it reaches the stage of the mature fruit, it is still the original seed. Thus, cause and effect do not shift; the beginning and the end penetrate one another.
This is indeed the essential gateway to the *Avataṃsaka*.

The Dharma-gate of the Ten Faiths consists of six chapters taught in the second assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*): first, the "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas"; second, the "Chapter on the Four Noble Truths";
third, the "Chapter on the Enlightenment of Light"; fourth, the "Chapter on Questions and Clarifications"; fifth, the "Chapter on Pure Conduct"; and sixth, the "Chapter on the Worthy."

The First Chapter. This section, in which Mañjuśrī is instructed to speak while relying on the Universal Radiance Palace (*Samantābhāsabhavana*), signifies that wondrous faith arises based on the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance and abides by means of the sublime discernment of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya*).
If one lacks this wisdom, one will only attain the vehicle of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) and will not be able to ride the Tathāgata-vehicle to achieve perfect enlightenment.

The Chapter on the Names of the One Buddha demonstrates that the names and traces of the Buddhas correspond to the Dharma and adapt to the capacities of sentient beings, such that they differ for each according to their respective minds.
As the Sūtra says: "All Buddhas know that the desires and inclinations of sentient beings are not the same;
they preach the Dharma and subdue them according to what is appropriate for each. Therefore, within this Sahā world, under one set of four continents, the Tathāgata manifests—
With various bodies and various names—some called Sarvārthasiddha, and so on, up to some called Śāstṛ—their number reaches ten thousand.
It is thus for one four-continent world system; it is likewise for the worlds of the ten directions, with ten thousand names for each.
It is thus for this Sahā world; it is likewise throughout the entire realm of phenomena and the realm of empty space.

The Chapter on Manifesting Various Bodies and Various Names and Titles. This section follows upon the forty questions raised by the bodhisattvas who gathered from other regions during the second assembly.
Regarding the first three lines of the sūtra, Qingliang divided them into ten questions: (1) the buddha-field; (2) the Buddha’s dwelling; (3) the adornment of the buddha-field;
(4) the dharma-nature of the Buddha; (5) the purity of the buddha-field; (6) that which the Buddha... [the text continues].
[The ten questions are: 1. The teaching of the Dharma; 2. The essential nature of the Buddha-fields; 3. The majestic virtue of the Buddhas; 4. The accomplishment of the Buddha-fields;

5. The Great Bodhi of the Buddhas. Qingliang [Zongmi] said: "These ten questions constitute five pairs. In each pair, the first phrase asks about the *parinirmita* (the environment), and the second phrase asks about the *sambhogakāya* (the primary retribution).
Furthermore, they proceed to ask about the ten abodes, the ten practices, up to the most supreme state of the Tathāgata and the light of the Tathāgata."
The *Ming* (Commentary) combines this with the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), forming thirty questions; when calculated together with the preceding, there are forty questions in total.

Fangshan’s edition takes the first three lines of the sutra as a single phrase, using the term "buddha-field" (*buddhakṣetra*) as the basis for the sentence; thus, it poses only four questions regarding the four kinds of buddha-fields, thereby omitting six questions.
It is appropriate to follow the Qingliang edition in establishing the phrasing. Within this first question concerning the buddha-field and the Buddha’s dwelling, [the text] asks about the Tathāgata.

This chapter is taught to answer [the question regarding] the spheres of activity and the spiritual powers of transformation; it also concurrently answers the previous inquiry concerning the ocean of Buddha-names.

By answering [the questions regarding] the Buddha-lands and the Buddha’s dwelling, it extensively clarifies how the Tathāgata’s body appears according to the lands and manifests names in accordance with sentient beings.
This is to cause those who enter through faith to know that the Buddha of their own mind has, from the beginning, pervaded the entire Dharma-realm. One.
Every place is nothing other than a Buddha-field; everywhere is nothing other than the dwelling of a Buddha. All names are the names of Buddhas, and all essences are the essence of Buddhas.
Thus, the wondrous contemplation of the *Avataṃsaka* manifests before one in every thought-moment.

These forty questions of the assembly are largely the same as, yet slightly different from, the thirty-seven questions of the World Ruler (*Lokanātha*). As for these repeated questions, the previous section was the "Section on Exhorting Practice by Citing the Fruit. Its...
Question: This is intended to clarify the dharmas accomplished as the fruit of Buddhahood; it serves as a therapeutic method for the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

The question is intended to clarify the dharmas that serve as the basis for causal practice. Since the dharmas accomplished as the fruit transcend verbal expression, the Tathāgata provides a general answer by manifesting signs.
However, since the dharmas relied upon in the cause must be introduced through detailed inquiry, Mañjuśrī speaks with words.
A separate answer follows. All the subsequent chapters provide sequential and distinct answers.

When about to expound the Dharma of the Ten Faiths, the Bodhisattvas from the ten directions each came from the presence of Buddhas of Ten Wisdoms in the worlds of Ten Colors—namely, the Golden and Equal-color worlds.
Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of a buddha-field have gathered together to manifest the ten causes and ten fruits of the gate of faith.
The fruits are the Buddhas of the ten wisdoms; the causes are the ten bodhisattvas, such as Mañjuśrī.

The ten colored worlds are the dharma-gates of practice, which essentially refer to all phenomena of form, clarifying the dharmas of one's own mind. These ten stages of the Dharma are all from the fundamental source.
It emerges from the essence of immovable wisdom (*acala-jñāna*). The remaining nine are all the functional manifestations of the virtue of immovable wisdom.
When one practices and progresses based upon this essence, there are ten stages; yet when these functions are subsumed back into the essence, they are but a single dharma.

This is the simultaneous union of quiescence and illumination, where cultivation and realization occur at once without further gradual succession. Therefore, the Sūtra mentions Buddhas and Bodhisattvas together to signify the identity of cause and fruit.
This is indeed manifest. However, when these positions are employed to symbolize the Dharma, they constitute the affairs of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

yet when they are understood as the luminous mind of the Dharma, they are all the inherent nature and virtue of human beings. The Dharma of the *Avataṃsaka* condescends to illuminate those with limited capacities;
do not defer to the sages and saints, claiming that you lack the portion [of this capacity] yourself. Thus, Master Sengzhao said: "How distant is the Sage? To embody him is itself the divine."

The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths demonstrates that the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma accords with the nature of reality and responds to the capacities of beings in various ways. As the Sūtra says:
"In the worlds of the ten directions, the Four Noble Truths are each spoken with four hundred *koṭi* of ten thousand names;
even throughout the entire Dharma-realm and the realm of empty space, the Four Noble Truths are each spoken with hundreds of millions of kinds of names. All of these...

According to the minds of sentient beings, he causes them all to be tamed. This clarifies that the Dharma taught by the Buddha all takes the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—as its essence.
Based on these Four Noble Truths, he expounds various teachings. Now, the nature is originally true and the Dharma is beyond verbal expression;
yet, through ignorance, karma arises, and the accumulation of suffering forms conditions. Having no choice but to act, the Sage responds accordingly to this.
Thus he taught the Dharma; therefore, all sutras take the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as their primary tenets.

This Dharma, which accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), likewise elucidates these at its outset. For it is from this [nature] that delusion arises and through this that [delusion] manifests; thus, when the sense faculties and their objects are liberated, the true luminosity of the original nature is revealed.
These are called the Four Noble Truths so that one may thoroughly understand the suffering and its origin within the mundane world.
The ultimate truth is such that, through rational penetration and integration, there is no longer any aversion or cessation. Like the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, it is without going or taking.
Taking this as the cause, the progression through all five stages is entirely of this same nature, and thus the fruit of Buddhahood can be attained.
This answers the previous question regarding the "Ocean of Exposition. (This chapter and the preceding "Chapter on the Names of Buddhas" together constitute one fascicle).
Regarding the "Chapter on the Awakening of the Three Radiant Lights": At the first assembly, the Buddha emitted the light of fruition from between his eyebrows;
having illuminated the ten directions, it entered back through the soles of his feet. Upon reaching this point, he again emitted light from beneath his feet.

This light illuminated one great trichiliocosm and extended to ten great trichiliocosms, gradually increasing in breadth until it pervaded the entire dharma-realm, causing those who have developed faith to awaken to the vastness of the Buddha’s realm of wisdom.
It is the Great Inexhaustible. One reverses this to realize that one’s own dharmakāya, wisdom, and practice are likewise entirely equal.

From this, one enters the five stages to open the eye of clear wisdom and attain the awakening of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*). Therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Awakening of Radiance.
As for the emission of the light of fruition from the feet, it symbolizes that the fruition and the causal practice mutually support and stimulate one another. Generally, from the cause...

To attain the fruit, one must necessarily possess the four dharmas of faith, understanding, practice, and realization. The first three chapters clarify faith; the latter three chapters constitute understanding, practice, and realization.
Regarding the fourth chapter, "The Chapter on the Clarity of Inquiry," Mañjuśrī and the Bodhisattva Navamukha engage in mutual dialogue to clearly elucidate the myriad dharmas.
This is to demonstrate the understanding of the ten stages of faith. At the outset, Mañjuśrī asks Jñānottara: "The nature of the mind is one;

how can there be distinctions between good and evil, suffering and pleasure, and karma? Jñānottara replies: "All phenomena have no functional activity; they exist only through the discrimination of the deluded mind.
When observed according to reality, all things are devoid of intrinsic nature. This intent clarifies that the essence of karma is fundamentally true, yet [sentient beings] turn their backs on it.
Because of awakening, there is delusion; yet when awakening arises based on the True, then all things are truly real. These ten Bodhisattvas clarify ten kinds of profound dharmas.
Bodhisattva Awakening Head clarifies the profundity of dependent origination; Bodhisattva Wealth Head clarifies the profundity of teaching and transforming.
Ratnamati elucidates the fruits of karma; Guṇamati elucidates the teaching of the Dharma; Netramati elucidates the field of merit;
Vīryamati elucidates the true teaching; Dharmamati elucidates right practice; Prajñāmati elucidates the aids to the path; Bhadramati elucidates the profound single path;
Mañjuśrī elucidates the profundity of the Buddha’s realm—all of these serve to manifest the truly pure essence of the Dharma. Following the ten questions, they are all concluded.
All the various phenomena of the dharma-realm and the realm of sentient beings are clearly manifested through the Buddha’s spiritual power;
therefore, it is called "Questioning for Illumination" (Wenming). (This chapter and the preceding "Illumination and Enlightenment" chapter [Guangming juepin] together constitute one fascicle.)
The "Chapter on the Five Pure Practices" extensively sets forth great vows as the practice for the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).

Its intent is that sentient beings, through ignorance and craving, become defiled by various worldly afflictions and lose the Buddha’s *Avataṃsaka*; this is due to a lack of the power of aspiration. Having now given rise to pure faith, [the practitioner proceeds].
One must rely on great vows to purify the afflictions (*kleśa*); indeed, it is precisely through the afflictions that pure conduct is accomplished.

Because the Bodhisattva Jñānaśrī posed one hundred and ten questions regarding how to attain the actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as all supreme and wondrous merits, Mañjuśrī expounded for him one hundred and forty great vows. To summarize: the Bodhisattva...
While living as a householder, one should wish that all beings be freed from oppression. In serving one’s parents with filial piety, one should wish that all beings protect and nourish all things.
From the moment of falling asleep until the first awakening, one should wish that all beings awaken to omniscience.

May they cause every mundane matter of affliction to be transformed into sublime practice. By means of these great vows, one purifies body, speech, and mind, thereby immediately attaining the One Vehicle.
All supreme and wondrous merits are thereby accomplished as the inexhaustible ocean of practices across the five stages.
No defiled phenomena can obstruct or hinder them; this is called "pure conduct. (This chapter shares one fascicle with the "Chapter on Worthy Leaders," Part One.)

The sixth chapter, "The Chapter on the Six Worthy Leaders," clarifies that by relying on the dharma-gate of the ten levels of faith, the merit of generating the mind and practicing advancement is immeasurable and equal to that of a Buddha;

it demonstrates the realization of the ten levels of faith. The sutra says: At that time, after Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva had finished expounding the great merit of pure conduct free from turbidity and confusion, wishing to reveal the merit of the bodhicitta, he questioned the Worthy One.
The first one said: "I have now already explained for the sake of all bodhisattvas the pure practices cultivated by the Buddhas in the past.

You, O Noble One (Bhadramukha), should likewise expound upon the supreme merits of practice within this assembly. Bhadramukha replied with a very extensive verse, fully detailing the merits of generating the mind of enlightenment and practicing, the increase and attainment of fruits, benefiting sentient beings and making offerings to the Buddhas, and even [the manner of] entering and exiting the various directions.
The Net Samādhi (*jāla-samādhi*). Manifestation and concealment occur simultaneously with sovereign non-obstruction;

all are identical to the fruition, practice, virtue, and function of Vairocana, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra. It reveals the dharmas of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the six stages (*ṣat-pada*).

When one arouses the bodhicitta and the understanding-practice (*adhimukti-caryā*) correspond, one has already attained this realization and immediately enters the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) from this point on. As for the Net Samādhi, first:
Entering right concentration in one direction while emerging from concentration in another;
entering right concentration in all directions while emerging from concentration in a single direction—just as in the Indra-net where they interpenetrate and harmoniously encompass one another.

Even entering right concentration within a male body and emerging from concentration within a female body is entirely like the Indra-net; for such is the fundamental nature and function of the Dharma-realm itself. Thousand...
They are of one substance, without duality or distinction; they differ only according to the perceptions of sentient beings.
If one realizes the Tathāgata’s nature of non-action, then entry and exit are sovereign; when the mind is without differentiation, the environment is likewise without differentiation.
The perfect realization of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) should culminate here. This constitutes the practice and realization of the "Worthy Head" (*Bhadramukha*).

Thus, one first enters the Buddha-nature from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); being adjacent to the ultimate and second only to the sages, they are called the "Worthy Head. Therefore, this section is titled the "Chapter on the Worthy Head.

From the "Chapter on Radiant Enlightenment" up to this point, all serve as answers to the question concerning the ocean of the Bodhisattva’s *prasthāna* (setting forth). This is because the five stages involve progressive advancement.
This proceeds from the arousal of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). (This chapter comprises two fascicles).

As for the "Ten Abodes" (*daśa-vihāra*): by virtue of faith, one realizes entry and is born into the family of the Tathāgata; because one relies on non-abiding wisdom (*apratiṣṭhita-jñāna*) and never regresses, it is called an "abode.
The Dharma-gate of the Ten Abodes was taught at the summit of Mount Sumeru in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven during the third assembly and also consists of six chapters.
1. Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru; 2. Chapter on Verses of Praise at the Summit of Mount Sumeru; 3. Chapter on the Ten Abodes; 4. Chapter on Brahma Conduct; 5.
Chapter on the Merit of Arousing the Mind; 6. Chapter on Elucidating the Dharma.
Regarding the "Chapter on Ascending Mount Sumeru": the location serves to symbolize the Dharma. The preceding Universal Radiance Hall (Samantaprabhā-śālā) represents the realm of the human world;
the teaching of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) based upon this realm symbolizes the initial generation of faith from the level of ordinary beings.
Now, Mount Sumeru is wondrously high and reaches the heavens; that the Ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) are taught here symbolizes ascending from faith to enter the vast and sublime limit.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Ten Abodes" states: "The dwelling place of the Bodhisattva is vast and expansive, equal to the dharma-realm and empty space.
This mountain stands upon the seven golden mountains and amidst the oceans, towering as high as the heavens; it is not something that can be ascended by grasping with hands or feet.

This signifies that the Dharma of the ten abodes emerges from the ocean of wondrous wisdom and transcends the realm of sensory objects; it is not something to be attained through the攀缘 (pān-yuan) [clinging/conditioning] of thought or mind. This chapter...
It clearly explains that [the Buddha] ultimately ascends and advances, and describes the matter of Śakra arranging a seat to welcome the Buddha. It further states:
"At that time, the World-Honored One, without departing from beneath the Bodhi tree, ascended Mount Sumeru toward the palace of Śakra.
Śakra prepared a lion throne of universal radiant treasury and invited the Buddha to sit upon it. This is the body of the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-kāya*).
It manifests everywhere according to conditions, just as the reflection of a single moon appears in a thousand rivers;
though it follows the north or south of the boat, it never truly comes or goes. Śakra invited the Buddha to recite ten verses of praise.
The first verse says: "Kāśyapa Tathāgata was endowed with great compassion; that Buddha once came to enter this hall. This continues until the tenth verse, which mentions Dīpaṃkara.
"The Great Radiance of the Tathāgata. That Buddha once entered this hall. The *Treatise* states: "The first three are Buddhas of the present kalpa;
the latter seven are Buddhas of previous kalpas. This clarifies that when [the Buddhas] first entered the Ten Abodes, the Buddhadharma of the ancient and modern eras was identical and not different.

The second chapter, "Verses of Praise by the Sumerus," features ten bodhisattvas, beginning with Dharmamati, who praise and manifest the dharmas of their respective stages and exhort others toward advancement.
Since the Ten Abodes take wisdom (*jñāna*) as their essence and insight (*prajñā*) as their function, one may advance only through them;
therefore, they are manifested through the praise of Bodhisattva Dharmamati. When about to expound the dharmas of the Ten Abodes, the ten bodhisattvas of insight from the ten directions...
Each of them came from ten worlds, such as Indra-flower and others, accompanied by Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of those lands.
These assemblies of Bodhisattvas had each, for ten months, purified their Brahma-conduct in the presence of the Buddhas. This represents the Dharma of the Ten Abodes:
relying on wisdom to give rise to insight as the cause, thereby further accomplishing the fruit of the Wisdom-Moon. Having attained this resultant Dharma, ignorance is suddenly [extinguished].
Thoroughly penetrating the afflictions, they are suddenly removed and become as cool as the moon. That Buddha represents the fruit and the Bodhisattvas represent the cause;
