this is also like the simultaneous manifestation of the causes and fruits of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). The "Ten Flower Worlds" are the very dharma-gates practiced;

in essence, they signify that the flowers of the cause have blossomed into the fruit of wisdom. The Sūtra says: "At that time, after the Bodhisattva Daśaprajñā had spoken these verses in praise of the Buddha..."
The Bodhisattva Dharmamati immediately entered the Samādhi of Immeasurable Expedient Means (*ananta-upāya-samādhi*).
From each of the ten directions, Buddhas as numerous as the atoms within a thousand Buddha-fields, all named Dharmamati, appeared before him in unison to offer praise and empowerment.

The treatise states that sentient beings possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, yet they are obscured by delusions and self-created hindrances; thus, anyone capable of cultivating expedient means—
To manifest that which was obscured, one enters into a profound union with the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas;
therefore, Buddhas bearing the same name appear universally before one.

In the "Chapter on the Thirty Abodes," the names and meanings of the ten abodes are correctly explained, demonstrating the practices to be performed at each respective stage. First, the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda*).
1. The Dwelling of Abiding (*vihāra*): Initially relying on correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) to give rise to the bodhicitta. 2. The Dwelling of Purifying the Ground (*bhūmi-pariśodhana-vihāra*):

To benefit sentient beings, one expands and broadens the ground of the mind. 3. The Dwelling of Cultivating Practice (*caryā-pratipatti-vihāra*): Skillfully contemplating all phenomena to increase correct practice. 4. The Dwelling of Noble Birth (*janma-udāra-vihāra*):
By means of noble conduct, one is born into the family of the Buddha-dharma. 5. The Dwelling of Endowment with Skillful Means (*upāya-saṃpanna-vihāra*): [Endowed with...]

1. True Conformity to Convention (*anuloma-saṃvṛti*) is the appropriate transformation through skillful means (*upāya*). 2. Abiding in the Right Mind (*samyak-citta-vihāra*) is the state where the mind remains unmoved when encountering objects that are either good or evil.

3. Abiding in Non-Retrogression (*avaivartika-vihāra*) is the state where the conditions for pursuing the correct and wondrous Way are not destroyed. 4. Abiding in Youthful Truth (*kumāra-bhūta-vihāra*) is the state where one contains the truth and embraces the One, so that wisdom and practice are never lost.
5. Abiding as a Dharma Prince (*dharma-rāja-putra-vihāra*) is the attainment of the Dharma of the Dharma King, whereby one is destined to succeed the Buddha.

This is the stage. The tenth, the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*), consists of accomplishing the ten knowledges, whereby one immediately becomes a Buddha, just as a royal prince undergoes the rite of consecration.
Regarding the text on the Ten Stages, each stage accomplishes ten dharmas to demonstrate the practice of that specific level;
furthermore, each stage encourages the study of ten dharmas to demonstrate the progressive excellence of each successive rank. The concluding passages for each of these ten sections state:

Upon hearing the Dharma, one immediately attains self-understanding without relying on the instruction of others. At the conclusion of the "Chapter on Establishing the Holy Life" (*Brahmacaryā-vyavasthāna-parivarta*), it further states:
"If bodhisattvas can accord with such contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-yoga*), the ocean of all Buddha-dharmas will simultaneously manifest before them.
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), they attain Bodhi. They know that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind."
The body of wisdom is accomplished not through awakening by means of another; this is intended to clarify that one’s inherent virtue should not be sought externally.
(This chapter, together with the two preceding chapters, constitutes one fascicle.)

Chapter Four: The Four Brahma-Vihāras. This clarifies that within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one observes ten dharmas: the body and bodily karma, speech and vocal karma, mind and mental karma, as well as the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts.

Among these, what constitutes the Brahma-vihāra? One knows that the three karmas of body and so forth, as well as the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena within the Buddha, Dharma, Sangha, and precepts, are all not the Brahma-vihāra. Thus, regarding the body, there is [no self].
Regarding what is grasped, one is unattached in cultivation; regarding phenomena, one dwells nowhere; even regarding the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there is no designation.
The mind is without obstruction, and skillful means are sovereign. This is called the pure holy life.

Furthermore, by citing the ten powers of the Tathāgata, one causes [the practitioner] to cultivate them according to their respective stages, as the method for accomplishing the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*).
Chapter Five: The Merits of Arousing the Bodhicitta. This chapter clarifies that the merits obtained through practicing the dharmas of the Ten Abodes are immeasurable.

The sutra employs more than ten metaphors to compare them repeatedly, yet they do not equal even a small fraction [of these merits], because the merit of arousing the bodhicitta is equal to the infinite ocean of fruition.
(This chapter and the preceding Chapter on Brahma-Conduct together constitute one fascicle.)

Sixth, the "Chapter on Clarifying the Dharmas" (*Liù míngfǎ pǐn*). Herein, the Bodhisattva Jingjìn Huì questions the Bodhisattva Fǎhuì regarding the practice of ascending to the next stage within this position, so as to make it even more clear and serve as the cause for the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*). Therefore, following this, the Dharma of the Ten Practices is expounded (this chapter comprises one fascicle).

Regarding the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*): Having relied upon universal wisdom to give rise to faith and abide in the dwelling of the Buddhas, one is thus able to extensively manifest the myriad practices for the sake of self-benefit and the benefit of others;
hence, the Ten Practices are taught. This Dharma-gate of the Ten Practices is expounded in four chapters in the fourth assembly at the Yāma Heaven:
first, "Ascending to the Yāma Heaven Chapter"; second, "Yāma Verses of Praise Chapter"; third, "Ten Practices Chapter"; and [the fourth].
The Fourth Section: The Storehouse of the Inexhaustible.

First, the Chapter on Ascending to the Yāma Heaven. *Suyāma* is translated here as "Good Time" (*shan shifen*). It is a heaven dwelling in space; it has neither sun nor moon, yet it is perpetually bright.
Day and night are distinguished by the opening and closing of lotus flowers; therefore, it is called "Good Time. Within this...

This exposition of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) signifies that practice is based upon the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*), remaining free from attachment while skillfully responding to the requirements of the occasion.
This chapter clarifies the advancement from the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and narrates the event of the King of the Yāma Heaven transforming his seat to welcome the Buddha.
The King of the Yāma Heaven requested the Buddha to speak, offering ten verses of praise; it is also stated that these were previously entered by the ten Tathāgatas.
This hall reveals that the principle and wisdom of the ten practices (*daśacaryā*) entered now are no different from those of antiquity.

Second is the "Verses of Praise by the Yāma Devas" chapter; herein, ten bodhisattvas, such as Guṇakusuma-vyūha (Gongde lin), praise and reveal the dharmas of their respective stages, exhorting and demonstrating advancement.
Because the accumulation of practice resides within them and their virtues provide broad shade, they are referred to as the Bodhisattva Guṇakusuma-vyūha.

"Sā" signifies manifestation. When he was about to expound the Dharma of the Ten Practices, bodhisattvas from ten forests in the ten directions—each from worlds such as Priyamedha and Brahmamedha, which possess the ten wisdoms—gathered together with bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of those lands. As for that assembly of bodhisattvas:
Each [bodhisattva] cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya) under the Buddha Daśanetra.

This stage is named "Forest" (*vana*) for Bodhisattvas to signify that from wisdom they give rise to practice, which provides shelter and gathers in those to be converted. It signifies the broad shade of sublime conduct.
Having already attained the eye of Tathāgata-wisdom at this stage, the Buddha is named after the "eye" to signify the use of the eye of wisdom to benefit sentient beings.
This also demonstrates the causal practice through which the ten practices are enacted; those who wish to practice these dharmas should do so.
(These two chapters and the "Ten Practices" chapter [in] the first fascicle constitute one volume.)
Chapter Thirty: The Ten Practices (*Daśabhūmika*). This chapter correctly explains the names and meanings of the ten practices and demonstrates the conduct to be practiced at each respective stage.
1. **The Practice of Joyful Resolve**: One gladdens oneself and others through the three kinds of giving: body, life, and wealth, as well as the Dharma. 2. **The Practice of Benefiting Others**:

One benefits all beings equally by means of the three groups of beings (*triskandha*) through the restraint of ethical discipline and the cultivation of wholesome dharmas. 3. **The Practice of Non-contradiction**: One endures and accords with sentient beings.

There is no contradiction with principle. Fourth is the practice of being unbending and unyielding: one exerts diligence toward the Way without retreat or weakness. Fifth is the practice of freedom from delusion and confusion:
through the clarity of concentration and wisdom, one is upright and free from all bewilderment. Sixth is the practice of skillful manifestation:

through *prajñā*, one perfectly illuminates the realm and wisdom, penetrating them with clear insight. Seventh is the practice of non-attachment: through *upāya*, one engages with the phenomenal world while remaining inwardly free from attachment.
Furthermore, the eighth is the practice of attainment, through which one is able to achieve the fulfillment of great vows.

The ninth is the practice of wholesome dharmas, by which one preaches the Dharma with the power of wondrous goodness to guide all things. The tenth is the practice of reality, whose essence is true wisdom and all that is authentic and truthful.
These ten practices take the ten *pāramitās* as their foundation; there is no practice that is not subsumed within them. (This chapter)

(Two fascicles in total). Section Four: The Treasury of the Inexhaustible. This explains the ten kinds of treasuries: faith, precepts, shame, dread of blame, learning, generosity, wisdom, mindfulness, retention, and eloquence.

The first seven are called the Seven Noble Riches; the [next] two serve as their guardians; and the last one is that which can be accumulated and then distributed. Furthermore, the first nine constitute the aggregates.
Accumulation. Subsequently, one gives rise to a single [practice]. Each and every practice, in its measure, contains within its essence the virtues and functions of the *dharmadhātu* without end;
therefore, it is called a "storehouse" (*kośa*). By means of this, the dharmas of the preceding ten practices are perfected, causing each practice to be inexhaustible;

the dharmas of the subsequent ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) are perfected, causing spiritual advancement to be inexhaustible. Therefore, following this, the ten methods of dedication are explained (this chapter comprises one fascicle).

Regarding the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*): in the preceding ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*) and ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the mind for transcending the mundane was predominant while the practice of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) was deficient.

Upon reaching this stage, one employs the wisdom of all Buddhas attained through the ten abodes and the world-transcending practices performed during the ten practices to supplement these with compassionate vows, thereby dwelling in the mundane world to benefit sentient beings.
One dedicates the ultimate toward the conventional and dedicates wisdom toward compassion, so that the ultimate and the conventional may be perfectly integrated.
Wisdom and compassion are non-dual, yet they are dedicated toward the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of bodhi. Universally penetrating the five stages, they benefit all beings;
this is called dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). Through this, wisdom, abandonment, and the virtues of grace are fully perfected, and the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya are thereby accomplished.
The Dharma-gate of the Ten Dedications is taught in the fifth assembly at Tuṣita Heaven and consists of three sections. First:
Chapter on Ascending to Tuṣita Heaven; Chapter Two, Verses of Praise in Tuṣita; Chapter Thirty, Dedication.
Regarding the first, the Chapter on Ascending to Tuṣita Heaven: *Tuṣita* is translated here as "Contentment.

Although this heaven does not transcend the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), it is called "Contentment" because its inhabitants are free from attachment to the objects of desire. This heaven is situated among the five heavens of the desire realm.
In this section, the exposition of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) symbolizes turning toward the conventional from the ultimate and turning toward compassion from wisdom.
Although one engages with the defilements of worldly toil, there is no attachment; one constantly abides in the Middle Way without falling into partiality or stagnation.
This chapter clarifies the advancement from the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and narrates the events of the King of Tuṣita Heaven preparing his seat to welcome the Buddha. The Sūtra says: "Tuṣita..."
The Celestial King led [the assembly] to his palace hall, where he had arranged a *maṇi* jewel throne with a hundred trillion tiers.
Each of its various ornaments and articles of offering numbered a hundred trillion. There were also a hundred trillion bodhisattvas, including those of the ten faiths and ten abodes;
as soon as they beheld this throne, each attained the benefit of the Dharma. This represents the dharma of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), which universally permeates the five [paths].
The stages are perfectly interfused and inexhaustible. The Dharma-seat of the Ten Abidings has hundreds of thousands of tiers;
the Ten Practices have one million; and the Ten Transferences have one hundred billion. These all symbolize the progressive advancement and increasing excellence of each stage.

Indeed, from the Ten Abidings up to this point, wisdom, practice, compassion, and vows are fully realized, and the Dharma of the Bodhisattva path is complete. Although there remain the final two stages...
Nothing is excluded from this treasury of Dharma. By universally dedicating all of this, its benefits, merit, and function become perfectly integrated and inexhaustible;
thus, each of the ritual matters and dharmas numbers in the hundreds of millions.

The King of Tuṣita Heaven also requested the Buddha to recite ten verses, citing ten Tathāgatas who had previously entered this hall. The treatise states that this clarifies the traces of the path of all Buddhas.
The essence is inherently pervasive and has not changed throughout past and present (this chapter consists of one fascicle).

Second is the "Verse Praise of Tuṣita" chapter: herein, ten bodhisattvas, including Vajradhvaja and others, praise and reveal the dharmas of their respective stages, exhorting and demonstrating the path of advancement.
This represents how the wisdom and compassion of this stage benefit sentient beings, destroy delusions, and subdue heterodoxy, while remaining naturally unshakable.
Because it is active, it is manifested through the praise of the Vajradhvaja (this chapter and the beginning of the *Pariṇāmanā-parivarta* share one scroll).
The *Triṃśat-pariṇāmanā-parivarta* correctly explains the names and meanings of the ten dedications and demonstrates the practices to be performed in each stage.
First, "Saving Beings while Remaining Free from Characteristics" means that great compassion provides universal relief while great wisdom remains unattached. Second, "Indestructible Dedication."
One attains indestructible faith in the Three Jewels and so forth. Third, "equal to all Buddhas" means training in the dedication practiced by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Fourth, "reaching all places" means that one's compassionate vows, activities, and conduct pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Fifth, "inexhaustible treasury of merit" means that by taking inexhaustible objects as conditions, one accomplishes inexhaustible merit and attains the inexhaustible.
This is the fruit. Sixth, "conforming to firmness" means that when one’s virtuous conduct constantly conforms to the firm and equal *dharmatā*, then all roots of goodness become entirely firm.
Seventh, "equally conforming to sentient beings" means benefiting things in accordance with them through a mind of equality.
Eighth, "the characteristic of *tathatā*" means that, realizing the essence of reality, one practices compassion without the mark of fabrication. Ninth...
One who is liberated without attachment or bondage does not cling to views nor is bound by signs, exercising sovereign mastery over all activities.
Regarding the "immeasurability of the ten dharma realms," this refers to the arising of function in accordance with the nature, transcending all measures.
This method of dedication, through the power of great vows, harmonizes wisdom and compassion, birth-and-death and nirvana, into a single dharma-realm of true selfhood.
Within the Dharma, it serves as the foundation for the fruits and virtues of the latter two stages; by integrating the former three stages, it forms the practice of the ten bhūmis.
Therefore, following this, the Dharma of the Ten Bhūmis is expounded (this fascicle comprises eleven scrolls).
Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmi*): they are so called because one accumulates the preceding dharmas until they reach their fulfillment, and all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon them.
As the Sūtra says: "Entering the practices of the various bodhisattva stages is that from which all Buddha-dharmas are born."
The Dharma-gate of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*) is taught as a single chapter in the sixth assembly at the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).

This heaven is the pinnacle of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). To teach the Ten Grounds based on this location symbolizes that the practices of the ten grounds depend upon the transformative manifestations for sentient beings and lack any self-natured transformation.
For while the preceding stage of the Three Worthies (*trayaḥ kalyāṇamitra*) was still for one's own benefit, these Ten Holy Ones consist purely of [the benefit of others].
Because it benefits others, there is no self-transformation. This stage has universal radiance wisdom (*samantāloka-jñāna*) as its essence;

that is to say, one has already trodden the Tathāgata’s Stage of Universal Radiance. Although the preceding four stages are not separate from this essence, because the merit of their accumulation was not yet complete, they could not be called "stages" (*bhūmi*).
This [stage], however, penetrates from beginning to end, and the practice of merit and action is now complete; thus, it encompasses the preceding four.
The stages merge into a single dharma; therefore, it is called the Ground of Wisdom of all Buddhas. From this point up to the eleventh stage, there is no further distinct dharma.
The treatise states: "These ten stages of dharma, from beginning to end, constitute a single gateway of the Dharma (ekānta-dharmamukha).
All these bodhisattvas are the assembly gathered like clouds, with Vajragarbha as their leader. Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority..."
Having explained the ten stages (*bhūmi*) for the sake of the assembly, [the Buddha] did not reveal their meaning, for the Dharma of the Buddhas' stage of wisdom is not bestowed lightly.
Then Vimukticandra, together with the assembly of bodhisattvas, made earnest requests three times, after which [the Buddha] finally spoke.

Therefore, it is said that the requester, the Dharma, the principal, and the retinue are present. Among this assembly, the first thirty-seven positions are collectively termed "Treasury" (*kośa*); only the final one is distinct.
The stage named "Liberation Moon" (*Vimukticandra*) signifies that this stage relies upon the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) to accumulate the preceding dharmas;

further aided by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), it becomes filled, vast, and fully perfected, thus being called a "Treasury. Upon attaining the full fruit, it is named "Liberation Moon.
As stated frequently throughout the various stages (*bhūmi*) in the sūtras: "Once the Bodhisattva dwells in this stage, by means of the Great..."

Through the power of their vows, they are able to see many Buddhas—namely, many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas, and even many hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddhas—and serve and make offerings to them all with a profound mind. This is because their merit relies on the perfection of the ground and their wisdom is fulfilled through their vows;
thus, they are able to mutually penetrate and pervade the realms of the Buddhas, and so they are able to see such a multitude.
The Buddha was served and made offerings to. Regarding the "Wisdom-Buddha manifesting from within the body of Vajragarbha":

when the sutra reaches the Dharma-Cloud Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), it describes the various, immeasurable powers of supernatural penetration and wisdom possessed by the Bodhisattvas of this stage. The great assembly all harbored doubts.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha entered the Samādhi of the Essential Nature of All Buddha-Lands. At that time, everyone in the assembly saw for themselves...

One’s body resides within the Body of Firm Concealment (*vajragarbha-kāya*). Furthermore, within that [body], beneath a bodhi tree upon a lion throne, there is a Buddha named Sarvajñābhijñārāja (King of All-Knowledge and Supernatural Powers), whose various marks of adornment are beyond the power of words to fully describe. The treatise states:
"The essential nature of all buddha-fields is the unconditioned *dharmatā*-kāya. The bodhi tree is the essence of awakening within *dharmatā*."

The "Wisdom-Penetrating King" (*Jitong Wang*) is precisely the wondrous wisdom within the *dharmatā*. It is inherently possessed by every person; it is simply that one has not applied personal cultivation to manifest it.

The fool says: if a practitioner were to manifest it for themselves, they would not only have no doubts regarding the supernatural powers and wisdom of a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*), but would sufficiently realize that all the Buddha-virtues expounded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are the constant nature of their own being.

[This is] a division. Regarding "the same names as the atoms of the lands": after the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha had explained the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), Bodhisattvas from each of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of ten Buddha-lands, all bearing the same name Vajragarbha, came from the presence of Vajradhvaja to serve as witnesses.

This signifies that the practitioners of this stage in the ten directions follow the same path; they are all on the ground of wisdom and, as the fruit of this stage, they crush and subdue all [obstacles].
The self-nature is immovable (this chapter comprises six fascicles).
The eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*) is the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*). It is called the eleventh stage because it transcends the ten stages.

This refers to one chapter spoken at the third dhyāna heaven during the seventh assembly. This is because the first dhyāna is free from sorrow and the second dhyāna extinguishes suffering; the third dhyāna alone...
This Dharma is a sublime and wondrous joy. It is based on this that the eleven stages (*bhūmi*) are taught;

this signifies that through the completion of progressive cultivation, one transcends all suffering and constantly enjoys the bliss of the Dharma. Its title is *Buddhāvatamsaka* (The Buddha-Flower). The text has not yet appeared [in its entirety].

It is called "Buddha-Flower" because, upon first ascending to the stage of Buddhahood, the fruits and practices are not yet fully perfected. Indeed, "flower" is spoken of in contrast to "fruit"; therefore, it follows...
This explains the practice for the fruit of Buddhahood (the Sanskrit original of this chapter is yet to come).
Reaching this point by way of the five stages, it answers the questions previously posed: the Ten Abodes answer the ocean of bodhisattva wisdom;
the Ten Practices answer the ocean of bodhisattva conduct; the Ten Dedications answer the ocean of bodhisattva vows; and the Ten Grounds answer the bodhisattva grounds.
It is an ocean. It is the ocean of transcendence for Bodhisattvas of the eleventh stage.
That is to say, the oceans of the Bodhisattva’s perfections, supernatural powers, vehicle, and factors conducive to enlightenment are all contained herein.

Next, from the chapter on the Ten Samādhis through the eleven chapters on the Inconceivable Lifespan and the Conduct of Samantabhadra, he answers the Buddha regarding the ocean of the Buddha’s lifespan.

The ocean of transformations and the ocean of Buddha-liberations have thus fully provided their answers. In the subsequent "Dharmadhātu" chapter, the five stages of cause and effect are perfectly revealed and reiterated;
likewise, the thirty-seven answers are also based upon this same perfect revelation and reiteration.
Now, as for the teaching of the Dharma of the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*), it begins with the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and concludes with the Third Dhyāna Heaven.
Regarding the deities who invited the Buddha, beginning with the preparation of the seats and ending with their being spread out:

because they abide in the abode of the Buddha and have not yet transcended that abode, the Dharma of the Ten Abodes was taught to the deities dwelling on earth, starting with those of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; thus, their seats were merely set in place.
It has not yet reached the stage of transformation (*nirmāṇa*). Every action is authentic and transcendent, utterly surpassing the mundane;

therefore, the Dharma of the Ten Practices was taught by [the Buddha] in the Yāma Heaven, which dwells in the void. Its seat is one of transformation, yet it has not yet reached the stage of full manifestation.
The True [Truth] is for one's own benefit; it is not that by which others are benefited. Transformation [Wisdom] relies on emptiness; it is not that by which one enters into existence.

One must necessarily turn back from the True to enter the conventional, mobilizing wisdom and practicing compassion, so that above one may transcend the realm of desire and below one may accord with the myriad things.
Therefore, among the five regions of India, the Dharma of the Ten Dedications was taught in Tuṣita. Its seat—

Thus, it is spread and distributed; it does not merely consist in being able to establish and transform. From this point on, its accumulated merit achieves fruition, as vast and expansive as the earth.

Its wondrous function manifests transcendentally, without relying on gradual stages. Therefore, the Dharma of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) is taught beyond the Heaven of Joyful Transformation (*nirmāṇarati*) in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*).
Beyond this, one enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), far surpassing all others.
One constantly enjoys the bliss of the Dharma amidst suffering; therefore, the dharmas of the eleventh stage transcend the second dhyāna and are explained within the third dhyāna heaven.
Every word and phrase of this symbolic teaching is not in vain. As for the statement that "the five stages reach perfection and the fruit of Buddhahood manifests before one," etc.:

The treatise classifies this as the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*). This is because, when one distinguishes the stages of abiding, practice, and progression (*sthiti-caryā-pratipatti*) within the ranks of the worthy and the noble (*ārya*), there are degrees of depth;
thus, while their merit is not yet perfected and their awakening not yet equal, although they are said to have "ascended the stages," this is the fruit of a bodhisattva, not the fruit of a Buddha.
By entering this position together with the four preceding dharmas, one becomes perfectly complete and equal, whereby the fruit of Buddhahood can be attained.
Thus it is. Following this, the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhaphala*) is explained.

The practice for the fruit of Buddhahood is the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). From the initial cause of the ten stages of faith (*shixin*), one passes through the five stages of the Dharma, cultivating and subduing afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
When these tendencies are exhausted and wisdom is luminous, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood by relying on this practice; this is the eighth assembly, the Universal Radiance (*Puguang*).

The Master [Zhi] Dian states that there are eleven chapters: namely, the Ten Samādhis, the Ten Supernatural Powers, the Ten Patiences, the Incalculable Eons, the Lifespan of the Tathāgata, the Abodes of Bodhisattvas, the Inconceivable Dharma, the Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies, the Merits of the Minor Marks, the Practices of Samantabhadra, and the Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata.
Qingliang states that the first six chapters clarify the perfection of the causes for Equal Enlightenment.

The final five chapters clarify the perfection of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment. As for the fact that both these causal practices of the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) and this resultant practice are taught in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*):
it demonstrates that when one first cultivates the practices of the *Avataṃsaka*, one relies upon the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) of the Hall of Universal Radiance to give rise to faith;

thereafter, as one progresses through the stages until the completion of practice and the fulfillment of the fruit, one never departs from that fundamental wisdom. This, then, is the relationship between cause and fruit.
Without departing from the original source, there is non-duality; throughout the three periods of time, it is a single thought-moment, with no transition between beginning and end.

This is to be in accord with the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom and to realize the ultimate fruit of the Dharma-realm, which is neither extinguished nor born. This is truly the great purport of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
The first is the "Ten Samādhis" chapter, which demonstrates that the essence of fundamental wisdom is common to both ordinary beings and Buddhas, serving as the source of quiescence and function.

Only a Buddha in the state of fruition can fully exhaust its subtlety; its virtuous functions are boundless, and it is designated as "ten" to manifest its perfection. The first is the Samādhi of Universal Radiance.
2. The Great Samādhi of the Light of Subtlety; 3. The Great Samādhi of Universally Visiting Buddha-lands; 4. The Great Samādhi of the Pure and Profound Mind; 5.
The Great Samādhi of Knowing the Treasury of Adornments of the Past; 6. The Great Samādhi of the Treasury of the Radiance of Wisdom; 7.
The Great Samādhi of Understanding the Adornments of All Buddhas; 8. The Great Samādhi of the Diverse Bodies of Sentient Beings; 9. The Great Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm.
The Great Samādhi. The Great Samādhi of the Ten Unobstructed Wheels. Regarding these ten samādhis:

they are the great essence of all Buddhas of the past and present, in which quiescence and function are sovereign and all-pervasive. Thus, the five positions are interfused to form a single dharma-body;

it is without beginning or end, non-transmigrating and immovable, wherein the one and many, the pure and mixed, and the identical and distinct are sovereignly interwoven. Therefore, the Buddha was about to expound these ten samādhis.

As for its name: previously, in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), he entered the Samādhi of the Limit of a Kṣaṇa. This demonstrates that the essence of this samādhi is entirely identical to the essence of universal radiance wisdom;
it is devoid of any further characteristics of past and present, extension and brevity, beginning and end, or shifting movement.
All these are suddenly perfected within the span of a single finger-snap. Therefore, it is called the "Samādhi of the Limit of a Kṣaṇa. Those who attain this samādhi are all capable of...

Accompanying Vairocana, the quiescence and function [of wisdom] are sovereign. This is precisely the essence of the fundamental wisdom shared by both sentient beings and Buddhas, as well as the source of its quiescence and function.
In this chapter, the Buddha himself speaks the names of the ten samādhis, while entrusting Samantabhadra to explain the functions of those ten samādhis.
This clarifies that the Buddha is the essence of fundamental wisdom, whereas Samantabhadra is the function of differentiated wisdom; these two are [inseparable].

Only then can one achieve mastery over quiescence and function. This assembly consists of one hundred stages; the first thirty are all named "Wisdom" (*prajñā*), while the subsequent seventy each have distinct names.
The treatise uses these thirty to represent the three gates of liberation (*trivimokṣa*) and the seventy to represent the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
This means that Bodhisattvas in these stages practice the seven factors of enlightenment based upon the wisdom of the three gates of liberation.

Practice. To awaken and benefit all sentient beings, their wisdom is identical, yet their practices differ. Nevertheless, the three gates of liberation and the seven factors of enlightenment are established for those at the initial stage of cultivation, yet are bestowed upon those in the stage of fruition.
This is the practice of the Sage who humbles himself to be one with all things.
Therefore, this chapter says: "The king of mani jewels can accord with whatever is requested, taking on the same color as the object, yet..."

"Having lost the virtue of one's own jewel" is a metaphor for attaining the fruit of the Jewel-King; though one benefits sentient beings according to their capacities and condescends to be like the common multitude, one does not lose the virtue of one's own fruit. (This chapter consists of four fascicles.)
Next is the "Chapter on the Ten Supernatural Powers" (*Daśābhijñā-parivarta*), which demonstrates the ten kinds of wisdom-powers arising from meditative concentration:

first, the power of knowing the minds of others; second, the power of the divine eye; third, the power of recollecting past lives; fourth, the knowledge of the future; fifth, the power of the divine ear; sixth, the power of traveling to all lands; seventh, the power of skillfully distinguishing languages;
eighth, the power of assuming countless form-bodies; ninth, the power of penetrating all phenomena; and tenth, the power of entering all states of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
This clarifies the opening of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) to form ten supernormal powers.

The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), psychic power (*ṛddhividhi*), and the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) each have two divisions, whereas the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) do not. Regarding the divine eye, there are two [types]:

the second refers to the present, while the fourth refers to the future. Regarding the divine ear, there are two [types]: the fifth refers to hearing well, while the seventh refers to discriminating well. Psychic power...

The "feet" (pāda) refer to the six and the eight; the six pertain to power and function, while the eight pertain to the manifestation of the body. "Exhaustion of outflows" (āsravakṣaya) refers to the nine and the ten;
the nine pertain to the exhaustion of outflows within wisdom, while the ten pertain to the exhaustion of outflows within meditative concentration.

All of these take unobstructed great wisdom as their essence, and are not within the reach of the lesser sages. This follows the "Chapter on the Ten Concentrations" to clarify the arising of function from concentration.
Therefore, there are these ten kinds of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).

Next is the Chapter on the Ten Patiences (*daśakṣānti*), which demonstrates the dharmas of patience in accordance with practice that encompass and transform others through skillful means. The fruition of practice reaches fulfillment here.

Regarding the statement that "one perfects patience by means of the supernormal knowledges, and the fruition of practice is completed at the end," the *Śāstra* says: "Prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one perfects the supernormal knowledges by means of patience."

After the eleventh stage, one achieves patience (*kṣānti*) through the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The former refers to the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*) cultivated progressively according to the stages;

this refers to the patience of the Dharma (*dharma-kṣānti*) that benefits sentient beings in accordance with practice. When the fruition of practice reaches this point, the conduct of Samantabhadra is fulfilled.

One is purely a Tathāgata of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), yet does not abandon the skillful means (*upāya*) of a bodhisattva. Therefore it is said: "The fruition of practice is fulfilled at the ultimate stage of wondrous enlightenment."

Regarding the "patience of the practice of reality" (*dharmakṣānti*), the Sūtra states that Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of patience, such as the patience like an echo, the patience like a shadow, the patience like a transformation, and the patience like space.
This means that while benefiting sentient beings through skillful means, in reality there is neither identity nor difference [between the means and the ultimate].

For example, an echo arises from conditions, yet it neither contradicts nor is mixed with the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, it is like the light and shadows of the sun appearing throughout all things.
In oil it is not oil; in water it is not water. In a river it does not float away; in a well it does not sink. It is not distinct from its single essence, yet there is "this" and "that.

It does not follow after objects as having distance or proximity. That Bodhisattvas differentiate two characteristics within non-dual phenomena, and that their skillful mastery, thorough penetration, and practice of the patience of following the Dharma are all likewise—this is what precedes [the following].

In the subsequent chapters there is no mention of the title "Bodhisattva"; thus, the meaning of the sutra has been taken to supplement it (this chapter and the preceding "Chapter on the Ten Universals" together form one fascicle).
Next are the "Chapter on the Incalculable" (*asaṃkhyeya*) and the "Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks," which clarify the two types of delusion regarding the dharmas of the Buddha-fruit.
These are what are called the delusion regarding vast calculation and the delusion regarding the merit of the secondary marks (*anuvyañjana*). These two are clearly understood only by the Buddha;

even Bodhisattvas remain deluded regarding them. Therefore, among the forty chapters of this sutra, only these two chapters were spoken by the Buddha himself, while all the others were spoken by Bodhisattvas of their respective stages.
The reason for clarifying vast calculation is to manifest the virtues of the Buddha.
It cannot be exhausted by calculation. Therefore, in the prose section, the immeasurability of the numbers that count is elucidated;

in the verse section, the boundlessness of the virtues being counted is elucidated. Thus, the *Saṃkhyā-varga* clarifies pervading all numbers, the *Āyus-pramāṇa-varga* clarifies exhausting all time, and the *Vihāra-varga* clarifies pervading all places. Regarding the discussion of *asaṃkhyeya*:
This alone is called "innumerable. This chapter cites all that is incalculable and inexpressible. Yet the Sūtra says:
"In this way, throughout the three periods of time without limit, all Bodhisattvas clearly appear.

This refers to the two types of delusion regarding the qualities of the Buddha-fruit, as explained in the "Chapter on the Qualities of the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-guṇa-parivarta*). If even Bodhisattvas are still deluded regarding these, it is only the Buddha who [is not].
It is clear and penetrating; therefore, it is called the "Dharma-gate of the Buddha-ground. This chapter is initiated by the inquiry of Bodhisattva Mind-King (*Cittarāja*).
From this point until the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata," it elucidates the vast sovereignty of the three karmas and two wisdoms of the Buddha-fruit.

This constitutes the perfection of patience through universal penetration. It brings about a mental activity as vast and sovereign as that of a king; therefore, it is initiated by relying upon the Bodhisattva Mind-King (*Cittarāja*).

Next is the "Chapter on Lifespan" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*), which clarifies the actual retributive lifespan of the Buddha-ground that accords with its true nature, extending through the inexhaustible time of the ocean of lands.
This transcends the realm of numerical calculation. The praise states: "By means of days and so forth, eons have neither cessation nor arising," and so on.
The sutra says: "At that time, the Bodhisattva Mind-King addressed the assembly, saying:
'One eon in this Sahā world, the Buddha-field of Śākyamuni, constitutes a single day and night in the Sukhāvatī world, the Buddha-field of Amitābha. Thus it is with Sukhāvatī.
One kalpa [in the world-system] is a single day and night in the Vajra-dṛḍha Buddha-field of the Kāṣāyadhvaja world.
In this manner, taking ten successive worlds, each takes one kalpa of the preceding stage as one day and night of the subsequent stage. As the Sūtra says:
In this manner, passing through a million *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, the single eon of the final world is made equivalent to one day and night of the preceding lands.
These are filled with great Bodhisattvas who practice alongside Samantabhadra.

This clarifies that the lifespan of the Buddha-ground’s true retribution, which accords with its nature, is inexhaustible, and that fundamental wisdom is without birth or extinction. This is due to...
The mental karma is vast and sovereign, thereby bringing about the vast sovereignty of the karmic life-span.
Next is the "Chapter on the Abodes of Bodhisattvas," which demonstrates that there is no direction in which they do not gather and transform beings, nor do they abandon the world;

thus it cites the eight directions—whether mountains or seas—to show that the holy ones dwell everywhere and are omnipresent. The praise says: "Their gathering and transforming of beings is without fixed direction," and so forth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mind-King addressed the assembly, saying: "In the eastern direction there is a place called Mount Ṛṣigiri.
Since ancient times, bodhisattvas have resided therein; currently, a bodhisattva named Vajravara dwells among a multitude of bodhisattvas, constantly preaching the Dharma within it.
In the southern direction there is a place called Mount Vijayakūṭa. In the western direction there is a place..."

These are named Mount Golden Flame; including Mount Fragrant Accumulation in the north, Mount Cool and Refreshing in the northeast, Mount Vajra in the ocean, Mount Stūpa in the southeast, Mount Radiance in the southwest, and Mount Fragrant Wind in the northwest—these total nine locations, all as previously cited.
Later, further extensive citations bring the total to twenty-two locations, of which these nine alone are [specifically] mentioned.
There are bodhisattvas with such names; this is merely a brief indication based on a single Jambudvīpa.

In reality, the dwelling places of bodhisattvas pervade the entire *dharmadhātu* and cannot be discussed in terms of specific locations. To speak thus is to clarify that the practices of Buddhas and bodhisattvas are all-pervasive;

they constantly propagate their teachings, acting without interruption or abandonment throughout the world. This is because their life-force and karma are vast and sovereign, thereby bringing about their enlightened activities.
Vast and sovereign, both the life-force and karmic actions are fundamentally rooted in the mind; therefore, all are taught by the Bodhisattva Mind-King (Cittarāja).
Mount Qingliang is the present-day Mount Wutai. (This chapter, together with the preceding two chapters, constitutes one fascicle.)

Next is the "Chapter on the Inconceivability of the Buddha," which clarifies that the dharmas of the Buddha-fruit—the wisdom and virtues—are profound and vast, transcending what can be conceived by ordinary consciousness.

Regarding the praise stating, "the inconceivable function within fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and so forth": the preceding section clarified the activities of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in gathering and transforming sentient beings;
this section clarifies the inconceivable transformative wisdom of the Buddha, which is not the realm of emotional consciousness.
Because it reaches beyond the scope of names and words, it is called "inconceivable.
This chapter was expounded by the Buddha’s spiritual power through the Bodhisattva Blue Lotus Treasury (Nīlotpalagarbha). He addressed the Bodhisattva Lotus Treasury (Padmagarbha);

the term "Blue Lotus Treasury" symbolizes that fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) is untainted and possesses discerning wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇa-jñāna). Furthermore, addressing him as "Lotus Treasury" symbolizes both fundamental wisdom and discerning wisdom.
Second is mutual accomplishment, which reveals the inconceivable and wondrous functioning of the mind and the Buddha;
this constitutes the vast and sovereign mastery of the two wisdoms (this chapter comprises two fascicles).
Next is the Chapter on the Ocean of the Ten Bodies. This clarifies that the primary retribution manifested through the gathering and transformation of great wisdom consists of ten kinds of bodies:

namely, the Body of Enlightenment (*bodhi-kāya*), the Body of Vow (*praṇidhāna-kāya*), the Body of Transformation (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), the Body of Sustaining Power (*anubhāva-kāya*), the Body of Marks and Signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana-kāya*), the Body of Majestic Power (*prabhāva-kāya*), the Body Born of Mind (*manomaya-kāya*), the Body of Merit (*puṇya-kāya*), the Body of Wisdom (*jñāna-kāya*), and the Body of Dharma (*dharma-kāya*).
Furthermore, there are marks as numerous as the atoms within the oceans of the Flower Treasury World-systems (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu-samudra-rajas*).
Because it is adorned with these, it is called the "Ocean of the Ten Bodies' Marks. It is commonly said that the thirty-two marks constitute the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
The *Sūtra of Contemplating the Buddha of Infinite Life* states that the eighty-four thousand marks constitute the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body).
Now, the marks numbering as many as the atoms within the ten Flower Treasury worlds constitute the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). This is praised as the inconceivable wisdom adorned with myriad virtues.
"Et cetera" (*ādi*): The Sūtra enumerates the ninety-seven marks of a Great Man up to body-marks as numerous as the atoms within ten Flower Treasury Oceans.

This is called the "Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies," adorned with myriad virtues. The Commentary states: "The preceding section explained the inconceivable function of the two wisdoms of the Mind and the Buddha;
this [section] demonstrates the inconceivable retribution of the two wisdoms of the Mind and the Buddha. Therefore, it is called 'Inconceivable'."
The Buddha is the fruit of the purification of wisdom.

Next is the Chapter on the Merits of the Minor Marks (*Anuvyañjana*). This clarifies that for every dust mote of a primary mark (*lakṣaṇa*), there are as many minor marks as there are dust motes. "Marks" refers to their physical forms;
"minor marks" refers to their beauty. Within each minor mark, there are manifold radiances, which are able to purify boundless realms and bring about liberation.
Regarding the intermediate offenses, their merits are inconceivable. As for the praise stating "the light-features, adornments, and inconceivable practices," the Sūtra says:
The Tathāgata possesses a secondary mark (anuvyañjana) named King of Perfection, which emits a great radiance named Pure Merit.

This light can illuminate as many lands as there are atoms, and according to the karma, conduct, and inclinations of all sentient beings, it causes them all to achieve fulfillment. By means of this...

By following right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) in practice, one destroys all hindrances and afflictions, thereby accomplishing this radiance. It adorns one's own body and simultaneously adorns other things;
therefore, it is called "adornment by the secondary marks" (*anuvyañjana*). "Secondary marks" follow upon the primary marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

The former clarifies that the retribution of wisdom accomplishes the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*); this clarifies that the retribution of conduct accomplishes the secondary marks. Therefore, it is said: "inconceivable purity of conduct."
The Buddha of Pure Fruit. These two chapters collectively manifest the vastness and sovereignty of the retribution of the three karmas and two wisdoms.
This chapter is addressed to the Bodhisattva Ratnapāṇi, signifying that the luminous nature of the Dharmakāya follows along with [the practitioner] to provide guidance and reception.

The next two sacred names are the narrative within this chapter (this chapter and the preceding "Ocean of the Ten Bodies" chapter constitute one fascicle). Next is the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra.
This clarifies the ocean of the Buddha’s conduct, which integrates the gateway of prior wisdom and extensively applies beneficial practices.

Regarding the praise that says "integrating the gateway of prior wisdom," this chapter extensively sets forth the dharma of Samantabhadra’s conduct, integrating the resultant wisdom of the preceding [stages] in order to enter [the ultimate state].
This benefits all beings. The shared practice of all Buddhas reaches its ultimate consummation in the fruit of the Tathāgata’s conduct;
therefore, following this, the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata" is taught. Regarding the Buddha Universal Banner (*Samantaketu*):

at that time, after Samantabhadra had spoken this Dharma, Bodhisattvas from worlds as numerous as the atoms of the lands of the ten directions, all named Samantabhadra, each came from the world Universal Victory (*Samantavijaya*) and the realm Universal Banner Sovereignty (*Samantaketu-vaśitā*).
The Buddha has come to this land to bear witness. This signifies the essence and function of the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Abiding in the path with humility and gentleness constitutes universal supremacy (*samanta-vijaya*). Subduing both self and others constitutes the universal banner (*samanta-dhvaja*).

Being fully endowed with wisdom, principle, compassion, and vows while responding to conditions constitutes sovereignty (*svatantra*). Advancing through the stages to their ultimate limit and silently establishing this path constitutes "coming to this land. Thus it is.
This serves as a testimony that the Buddha’s Samantabhadra practices pervade all places; that throughout the ten directions, those on the same path are non-dual and inexhaustible.
(This chapter consists of one fascicle.
Next is the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Tathāgata. Regarding the Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising at the beginning: this is the foremost of faith.
Mañjuśrī, under this alternative name, inquires of the Tathāgata regarding the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s manifestation.
He demonstrates that one proceeds from the ten stages of faith, relying on wisdom for further cultivation, until the practices of worldly and world-transcending wisdom and compassion are perfected.

At that point, the Tathāgata of Original Wisdom arises from self-nature with wondrous virtues fully complete; therefore, he inquires as the Bodhisattva of the Tathāgata’s Nature-Arising Wondrous Virtue.
The manner in which the Tathāgata appears is the integration, as discussed in the preceding chapter, of the perfection of the three karmas and two wisdoms into a vast and sovereign state.

Furthermore, regarding the praise that "the self-nature Tathāgata is moistened by the rain of Dharma," the Sūtra explains that the appearance of the Tathāgata possesses ten kinds of immeasurable marks of beneficial conduct (*anugraha-karman*), the tenth being the "Voice."

The *Xiāngyún* (Cloud of Characteristics) states: When the Tathāgata desires to teach and transform sentient beings through the True Dharma, he first spreads clouds of his body to pervasively cover the Dharma-realm.
He manifests various kinds of light and lightning flashes, and produces the thunderous sound of immeasurable samādhis.
From a heart of unimpeded compassion, he raises the great wind-wheel of wisdom; thereafter, from the clouds of the Dharmakāya, he rains down the rain of Dharma extensively. What... [text continues]
That is to say: for Bodhisattvas sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), he rains down the rain of the non-differentiated Dharma-realm;
for Bodhisattvas in their final birth, he rains down the rain of the playful, secret teachings of the Tathāgata;

even for those seeking the vehicle of the Pratyekabuddhas, he rains down the rain of the profound realization of dependent origination, which avoids the two extremes and possesses indestructible liberation; and for those seeking the [Śrāvaka]...
Regarding those who hear of the Vehicle: they rain down the sword of wisdom to sever the enemies of affliction with the Dharma-rain. Other matters need not be further enumerated;
all clarify that the self-nature Tathāgata’s merit is perfected, his wisdom manifests, and he performs effortless, limitless, and sovereign acts of beneficial conduct.
Next, regarding the two classes of those who receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood:

after the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra had expounded the Dharma of the appearance of the Tathāgata, Tathāgatas from as many lands in the ten directions as there are motes of dust—each bearing the same name as Samantabhadra—came to bear witness. They further spoke these words:
Now, among those in this assembly, there are Bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms of the lands of the ten directions who have attained all the supernatural powers and samādhis of Bodhisattvas;

I bestow upon them all the prediction that they shall attain Bodhi in one more lifetime. Furthermore, there are sentient beings as numerous as the atoms of the lands who have resolved their minds toward Bodhi;
I likewise bestow upon them the prediction that after an incalculable number of kalpas, as numerous as the atoms of the lands, they shall all attain Buddhahood.
This is titled "The Supreme Realm. This clarifies that once one has personally practiced and attained the fruit, those beings whom one transforms shall likewise attain the fruit.
Regarding Bodhisattvas, it is called "one lifetime," because their faculties and capacities are already matured and they easily achieve transcendence.

Regarding ordinary sentient beings, it is called "aeons as numerous as motes of dust," because their delusions have accumulated for so long and their transcendence is difficult. These are merely spoken in accordance with their specific capacities. At [the end of the passage],...

Within the true nature (*dharmatā*), the past, present, and future are one and the same; the three periods of time are a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*). Thus, sudden realization in a single instant constitutes a lifetime.

Furthermore, by means of the samādhi of a single instant, the ocean of the Tathāgata’s correct wisdom is manifested; consequently, delusions spanning boundless kalpas are suddenly extinguished in a single moment.
This is what is meant by attaining Buddhahood after passing through unspeakable numbers of kalpas, and it is called the "Exalted Realm" (*viśeṣa-viṣaya*).
As for the "Dhātu" (Realm), it is so called because it transcends the sphere of conceptual calculation.

Now, beginning with Mañjuśrī’s arousal of faith, one progresses through the stages of cultivation until the fruit of Buddhahood is realized at the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*). Furthermore, from the originally inherent, fixed essence, one gives rise to function;

according to practice, one achieves patience (*kṣānti*), penetrates the two delusions, enjoys the lifespan of true retribution, and performs boundless, universal transformation and guidance. It is not... [the text continues].
Having abandoned the mundane world, one accomplishes inconceivable wisdom and attains the retribution of the ten bodies.

Furthermore, through the perfect integration and vast benefit of Samantabhadra’s great practices, the virtues of the Tathāgata of self-nature are thereby made most manifest; previously, they were obscured by delusion.
It is only upon reaching this point that [the Buddha] manifests; therefore, the final chapter is titled "The Appearance of the Tathāgata," which encompasses both the fruit and the practice.

Furthermore, the "Leaving the World" chapter explains the constant way of benefiting sentient beings after the realization of the fruit. These together constitute the section on the establishment of the Dharma for the cultivation and realization of the habitual tendencies (this chapter comprises three fascicles).
The first thirty-one chapters of the *Qingliang ke* constitute the "Section on Cultivating Causes to Accord with the Fruit and Generate Understanding.

The chapter "Leaving the World" constitutes the "Section on Relying on the Dharma to Advance in Practice and Accomplish Conduct. This concludes the explanation of the second of the three cycles of teaching.

The tenth assembly of the third cycle, the chapter "Entering the Dharma Realm," describes Sudhana’s journey southward, wherein he is once again instructed on the causes and effects of the five stages (*pañcāvasthā*).

This section is titled "Distinguishing the Portion of the Dharma Realm" because it manifests the perfection of practice based on the words previously taught. While the preceding sections explained and demonstrated the dharma-gates, this section intends for one to embody them through practice;
therefore, it relies on Sudhana’s renewed instructions. Furthermore, as the merit of previous cultivation has reached its conclusion, the reliance on verbal explanations is forgotten.
One suddenly realizes and enters this Dharma-gate; therefore, one speaks of departing from words and relying on practice. As for the text of this chapter:
when extended outward from the cause, it reveals Sudhana’s journey through the hundred cities; when contracted inward from the fruit, it reveals Maitreya’s pavilion.

Thus, the practices of the five stages and the principles and phenomena of the Dharma-realm are fully realized through direct observation. This is called the perfect manifestation of the Dharma-realm. Relying upon this—
It is called the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma Realm" (*Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta*) because it describes the realization and entry [into the realm].
It was spoken at the final location, the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. This grove is located in the human world of the Western Regions.

By teaching the "Dharma Realm Chapter" in this place, it demonstrates that the Buddha-dharma realm is not separate from the human world. All those assembled in the assembly of the Dharma Realm silently manifested spiritual transformations.

This serves to manifest the fruition of practice. The assembly present, following this silent indication, likewise all silently attained samādhi; this is the meaning of departing from words to rely upon practice.

For if one remains stuck in verbal explanations, one will ultimately remain deluded regarding one's own realization; yet without practice, one will ultimately fall into mere狂解 (mad or delusional understanding).
Therefore, at the very end, a separate dharma-gate of "departing from words to rely upon practice" was established, entrusting [the teaching] to Sudhana’s journey to the south.
Regarding the traces of his practice: even when returning to his official position, he did not cease his cultivation; he established rituals and left behind models for others to emulate.
Having attained this Way, he was simply able to practice with composure and flow naturally, thereby entering the wondrously adorned ocean of the Buddha-dharma realm.
Yet those who are deluded merely cling to the name of "transcending words," becoming confused about the reality of relying on practice, and hastily advocate the cessation of study.

To take the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as right and to take the true cultivation of the correct path as wrong leads ultimately to self-reproach, the neglect of the teachings, and the forgetting of practice.
Thus, one becomes dissolute and without foundation; consequently, the *Avataṃsaka*’s actual discourse on dharmas that accord with the nature of reality would all be rendered a hollow fabrication.
Such people—foxes who deny existence and dogs that chase clods of earth—are proliferating throughout the world. Let students reflect with care.
The *Qingliang* commentary designates this single chapter as the "Section on Entering through Human Testimony to Accomplish Virtue. The preceding explanation concludes the third cycle of the Dharma.
The major headings consist of two types of eternal paths.
"Being unstained by the common dust while constantly benefiting sentient beings" refers to the constant practice following the attainment of the fruits of the five stages of progressive cultivation.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that practicing with a beginner's mind is like clarifying turbid water: when it is still, deep, and unmoving, the sand and silt naturally settle.
This is called the initial subduing of adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*). When the mud is removed and the water is pure, it is called "perpetual severance."

Fundamental ignorance: at present, as the five stages have not yet concluded and meritorious practice is not yet perfected, it is like sand and soil that, though they settle, become turbid when stirred;
thus, one cannot yet be said to be "identical with the dust. When merit is accomplished and practice is fulfilled, it is like removing the mud so that there is pure water;

no matter how much it is stirred or churned, it will never again be defiled or turbid. Therefore, only after the completion of the meritorious work of progress and cultivation does one subsequently manifest identity [with the world].

Unstained by the dust [of worldly phenomena], this is the constant path for benefiting sentient beings. This is the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva, who employs the practices of Samantabhadra to enter the marketplace and benefit sentient beings.
It is an effortless, unceasing, intentionless, and selfless practice of universal equality and sovereignty; therefore, it is called the "constant path.

This refers to the "Chapter on Transcending the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) preached in the ninth assembly at the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*). This chapter follows the Tathāgata.

Regarding the fact that the "Chapter on Manifestation" (*Prakāśana-parivarta*) was also preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā-vimāna*): it demonstrates that when the merits of the five stages are perfected, the *svabhāva-tathāgata* manifests;
yet, returning to the fundamental wisdom of universal radiance, one gives rise to birth while dwelling in the world without defilement. Therefore, it is named the "Chapter on Transcending the World.
Ordinary beings are defiled by the world and cannot escape it; although those of the two vehicles have transcended it, they are unable to accord with it. It is not...
This is true detachment. Herein it is clarified that when one practices compassion within the fruit [of enlightenment], one can follow worldly wisdom without being defiled;

thus, while constantly remaining in the world, one has never failed to be detached. There has never been a perception of purity, let alone perceptions of defilement. Only when both following and detaching are simultaneously extinguished does one truly transcend the world.
Within this text, two hundred questions arise like clouds from Samantabhadra’s Universal Wisdom, and they are answered by Samantabhadra pouring forth [the teaching) like water from a flask.

The *Qianchou* (Thousand Answers) clarifies all of this. Next, the praise states: "Benefiting sentient beings through constant practice, abiding in the ten dharmas, and constantly beholding the ten Buddhas.
This refers to the two hundred questions in the *Puhui* (Universal Wisdom) chapter, which asks:

"What is the preaching of the Buddha? What is the seeing of the Buddha? In response, Samantabhadra says: "A Bodhisattva constantly speaks of the ten Buddhas; that is to say, the attainment of perfect enlightenment..."

The Buddha of Non-attachment is seen through the vision of non-attachment; the Buddha of Birth is seen through the vision of aspiration; the Buddha of Karmic Retribution is seen through the vision of deep faith;

the Buddha of Sustenance is seen through the vision of compliance; the Buddha of Nirvāṇa is seen through the vision of profound entry; the Buddha of the Dharma-realm is seen through the vision of universal arrival; the Buddha of Mind is seen through the vision of peaceful abiding.
One sees the Samādhi Buddha as immeasurable and non-reliant; one clearly sees the Innate Nature Buddha; one universally receives the vision of the Buddha of Joyful Accord.
If a bodhisattva abides in this Dharma, they will constantly behold the unsurpassed Tathāgata. This means:
being unattached to perfect enlightenment, giving rise to compassionate vows, engendering faith in karmic retribution, and acting in accordance with the sustaining power [of the Buddha].
He enters deeply into nirvāṇa; he reaches everywhere throughout the dharma-realm; his mind dwells in tranquility; he relies on nothing within samādhi;

he clearly realizes his own fundamental nature; and he universally bestows according to the inclinations [of beings]. "According to inclination" means responding to each being in accordance with what they desire.
One who can rest securely in this Dharma will find that there is nothing that is not the Buddha, and nothing that is not seen as the Buddha.
Therefore it is said: "He constantly speaks of the ten Buddhas and constantly sees the ten Buddhas" (this *Lishi jianpin* [Chapter on Leaving the World] comprises seven fascicles).
The *Yuanzhang zhongyu zhu* (*Commentary on the Repeated Explanations of the Perfect Manifestation*) is divided into five sections.

First, regarding the assembly that fully manifests the sphere of practice, the praise states: "Forgetting verbal designations, one suddenly realizes [the truth], with a single thought encompassing all.
This refers to the initial assembly gathered at the site of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). It represents the five stages of the path without differentiating them into five distinct stages;

its intent is to reveal that by forgetting prior verbal designations, one suddenly realizes the sphere of practice, wherein a single thought encompasses everything without further gradual progression. Second, the same assembly.
I request the assembly of Dharma-practitioners. Regarding the praise "forever emerged from the ocean of existence, the five hundred śrāvakas":
this refers to the śrāvakas, bodhisattvas, and world-protectors manifested within this Dharma-realm assembly who collectively requested the teaching of this chapter.

Thus, Śāriputra and the others are listed by name at the end. The sutra praises their virtues, saying: "Forever emerged from the ocean of existence, dwelling in the state of non-obstruction; regarding the Buddha..."
The Ocean of Wisdom enters with deep faith. Furthermore, it is praised as "the one who constantly benefits sentient beings, the Lord of Immeasurable Worlds.
The Sūtra extols his virtues, saying: "He constantly benefits sentient beings as an uninvited friend. This refers to a Bodhisattva of great expedient power manifesting as a worldly lord.
Regarding the assembly gathering from the thirty directions, it is praised as "silently indicating the fruit of Buddhahood," referring to the preceding assembly.
Once they had assembled, they questioned the Tathāgata regarding ten dharma-gates concerning the realm and wisdom [of the Buddha].
At that time, the World-Honored One, through the skillful means of great compassion, entered the Lion’s Yawn Samādhi. All worlds were universally purified and adorned.
From each of the ten directions, a bodhisattva came from a buddha-field, each manifesting inexhaustible dharma-gates. First, from the east...
Within the assembly of the Buddha Vairocana-Guṇarāja, there was a bodhisattva named Vairocana-Prāṇidhāna-prabhāsa.
He eventually reached the assembly of the Buddha Samantajñānacakra-prabhāsa-ghoṣa above, where there was a bodhisattva named Dharmadhātu-vibhakti-praṇidhāna.
Each arrived accompanied by as many bodhisattvas as there are atoms in a buddha-field. Each performed various kinds of buddha-activities and offerings:
some displayed the adornments of celestial palaces (*kūṭāgāra*), some displayed the adornments of precious grounds, and some displayed the adornments of physical forms;

they even manifested the entire ocean of practices of all Buddhas of the three periods of time, pervading the entire dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This silently reveals the fundamental nature of the fruit of Buddhahood within the dharma-realm.
"Practice. This answers the previous question. The reason for this silent indication is that it intends to cause one to move beyond verbal expressions and silently cultivate the realm of practice.
"The lion’s stretch" refers to the appearance of moving the countenance with spontaneous ease, characterized by sovereign freedom and fearlessness.

This metaphor illustrates how this samādhi, relying on the sovereignty of non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-jñāna*) within the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), spontaneously manifests vast and sublime virtues and functions.

Fourth, regarding the manifestation for the assembly that has realized the Dharma: the praise states, "Deeply entering the ocean of wisdom, manifesting equality amidst the flow of delusion," and so forth.
This refers to the assembly of śrāvakas; although they were present at the same gathering due to the previously revealed silent teaching of the Dharma, they all [remained unaware].
They are indeed able to see it. However, the previous praise of their virtues stated: "With deep faith, they enter the ocean of the Buddha’s wisdom. How could they truly be deluded beings?

This was merely a demonstration that they were as if unable to see, in order to reveal that the sphere of practice is inconceivable and to lead all followers of the Hīnayāna to enter therein together.
Fifth, regarding the group who silently realize the sphere of practice, the praise says: "Having received the illumination of the Buddha’s light, they do not rely on..."

Regarding the phrase "the explanation of words, etc.": since the śrāvakas were confused regarding the sphere of practice, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause the bodhisattvas to dwell securely in the Lion’s Yawn Samādhi, emitted a ray of light from the tuft of hair between his eyebrows, named "The Door of Universally Illuminating the Dharma Realm of the Three Times.
At that time, the assembly, by means of this light, beheld the various names and forms of the oceans of lands, as well as the various manifestations of Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, they all entered this samādhi. They were also able to extensively manifest various kinds of entry into the unspeakable ocean of the Buddha’s spiritual transformations;
all of these were attained through silent resonance without relying on verbal expression, as they pertain to the sphere of practice.

The treatise concludes that the above constitutes the complete answer to the previously asked question regarding the dharma-gate. This entire scripture is the perfect embodiment of the essence of the Dharma-realm from beginning to end. By means of...
The lower section provides a profound exhortation and further clarifies the sphere of practice.

Second, regarding "forgetting cultivation and severing realization to manifest the Buddha-fruit, the eternal Way": this is the virtue of returning to the root and restoring the source, the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) within the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
These two paths are one and the same; however, while the former demonstrates cultivation and realization, this demonstrates...
There is no cultivation. The preceding stages constitute the practice for those in training; this constitutes the practice of the Buddhas.
It is the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the tenth assembly, wherein the causal wisdom-practices of the preceding stages are universally integrated into a single Dharma-realm.
This is called the gate of effortless, great function, perfect fusion, and sovereign mastery. To illustrate this, Sudhana travels south, beginning his journey upon the path of the ancient Buddhas.
He traveled extensively through a hundred cities to visit spiritual teachers, ultimately attaining perfect realization of the path of Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra.
His intention was to synthesize the realms of cause and effect of the Buddhas of the three periods of time into a single moment, a single limit, and the one true Dharma-realm.
This is to manifest that every person inherently possesses wondrous virtue, which is fully complete, perfectly interfused, and sovereignly free;
thus, it serves as the eternal Way of the Buddha-fruit, wherein cultivation is forgotten and realization is transcended.

Indeed, the sutras in their hundreds of fascicles and the teachings on the five stages are for the purpose of subduing habitual tendencies and advancing in practice, looking downward to clarify this inherently existing virtue. For when a practitioner has not yet resolved their mind toward enlightenment, they possess nothing [of this virtue].

It clarifies that because habitual tendencies and afflictive obstructions veil the fundamental wisdom, one employs the methods of the five stages to refine and purify it repeatedly until its brilliance reaches its ultimate limit.
Once this brilliance is perfected, there is no further need for cultivation or effort; it is like polishing a mirror:
when the grime is exhausted and the clarity appears, the function of polishing ceases. Therefore, at the very end, the Way of forgetting cultivation and transcending realization is taught.

And so it concludes. Yet, it is but a single stage of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). While previously it was judged as "departing from words" based on practice (*pratipatti*), here it is judged as "forgetting cultivation and severing realization.
This stage comprehensively perfects the preceding teachings; in principle, nothing is lacking.

It is merely distinguished according to the intended meaning of what is being accomplished, using the three cycles of cause and effect as a metaphorical basis for clarification, desiring to suddenly forget all linguistic designations.
Therefore, it is established that one proceeds by relying on practice through the elimination of words. These two kinds of eternal paths are realized through cultivation;

yet, because one desires to return to the root and revert to the source, it is established that one achieves this by forgetting cultivation and severing realization. There are varying depths in these sequences, and each intention has its appropriate application.

This is not contradictory. To summarize and synthesize it: the preceding thirty-eight chapters begin with the assembly gathering, the proclamation of the fundamental principle, and the presentation of the fruit that inspires faith;
they proceed through the five stages to realize the two types of enlightenment, and conclude with the eternal way of benefiting sentient beings while remaining unstained by worldly dust.
This is the true model for practicing and realizing the fruit, beginning from the stage of an ordinary person and culminating in the attainment of Buddhahood.

The final chapter, which discards words to rely on practice and forgets cultivation to sever realization, serves to sweep away the mind’s lingering traces of verbal expression and restore the full perfection of virtuous function.
It is a state of vast oblivion to conditions, a transcendent self-attainment that constitutes the essential core of this entire scripture and the profound source of the Ultimate Way.
Compared to the preceding texts, those are like the myriad rivers, while this is like—

The great ocean: once one has reached this, then the former distinctions of shallow and deep, source and stream, identity and difference, and all such boundaries vanish entirely and can no longer be perceived.
This is the ultimate consummation of the Flower Treasury Sea of Teachings. Furthermore, these are profound expositions based on metaphorical traces.
This is the site where Sudhana traveled southward. Following the same fundamental principle as before, it further elucidates the intent of the One Treasury (Ekakṣaya).
The reason for this re-elucidation is that while the former section explained and demonstrated the Dharma-gates, this one intends to embody and practice them.

The essential point of such embodiment lies in silent realization that does not involve verbal explanation; therefore, among the various stages and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), those who symbolize the Dharma are frequently seen.
Within the space of a single movement, the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī of the Ten Abodes strolled slowly in perambulation upon a separate mountain to demonstrate the non-duality of quiescence and function;
the Bhikṣu Sudarśana of the Ten Practices performed perambulation within a forest to demonstrate that wondrous conduct is without abiding;
and the Elder Gandhakuṭi of the Ten Dedications blended various incenses to demonstrate the perfect fusion of wisdom and compassion.
