The Night Goddess of the Tenth Ground manifests in a female body during the springtime to demonstrate the nurturing of great compassion.
The Lady Māyā, through her illusory manifestation on the Eleventh Ground, demonstrates the realization of wisdom at the conclusion of compassion as she passes away within the pavilion of Maitreya.
In the space of a single finger-snap, he suddenly reveals the infinite phenomena of the Dharma-realm throughout the ten directions.
From the subtle to the manifest, he seeks to embody them in silence, without resorting to verbal explanations; though there are words within this process, they are merely the dregs of expression.
For while words can explain the Way, they can never exhaust it; thus Confucius said, "Words do not exhaust meaning," and established images to convey it.

He exhausted [all means of expression], yet the Patriarch still considered this insufficient. Thereupon, he cast aside names, words, forms, and appearances, attaining realization solely in the moments of striking the gavel or raising the whisk.
At that very moment, speech, silence, form, and appearance were beyond the reach of description;
this was truly the ultimate, the absolute. One who traverses the Dharma-gates of the fifty-three spiritual friends should act accordingly.
This is the section on "Entry. It is further divided into five parts.
The first concerns the assembly of beginners who have newly begun their practice. The eulogy states: "From the fundamental wisdom, those who have first awakened [are praised].
This praises the virtue of Mañjuśrī’s skillful means (*upāya*). As the Sūtra says: "At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī emerged from the Hall of Good Abiding (*Susthitakuṭa*)."

Together with immeasurable fellow-practicing bodhisattvas and the eight classes of devas who constantly attend him, he paid homage to the Buddha, took his leave, and traveled south toward the human realm.
The commentary states that this signifies the arising of differentiated wisdom from the fundamental wisdom of the dharmakāya;

it marks the initial practice for enlightening sentient beings in accordance with worldly conventions. This is the stage of faith within the gate of practice (*caryāmukha*), serving as the foundation for all [beings] within the dharma-realm.
This is the beginning of the Buddha’s initial resolve for practice; it is the first awakening of the fundamental wisdom of the *dharmakāya*.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī is here referred to as a "child" (*kumāra*), signifying that the initial mind of an innocent seeker awakens from this point onward.

Nevertheless, in the preceding stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), Mañjuśrī was designated as the "foremost of faith" and called a Bodhisattva; whereas in this stage of faith, Mañjuśrī is designated as the "awakening of the ignorant."

The "youth" (kumāra) is the gateway for prior cultivation; it is the desire arising from the mind that seeks to understand the cause and proceed toward the fruit—this is the gateway for creating awakening.

It is the desire for understanding that ultimately leads to practice and personally receives enlightenment. Because the stages of awakening and cultivation differ, they are designated by different names according to their sequence;
yet, within the essence of wisdom, there is from the outset no difference whatsoever.

Regarding the second group, those who follow through their practice and resolve: as for the praise stating that they "observe sublime conduct and resolve upon bodhicitta," this refers to the time when Mañjuśrī traveled southward.

Six thousand śrāvakas vowed to follow Mañjuśrī, and along the way, Śāriputra had the bhikṣus, such as Sāgarabuddhi and others, observe the various sublime virtues of Mañjuśrī; thereupon, Mañjuśrī exhorted them.
Generating the bodhicitta and abiding in the conduct of Samantabhadra, one immediately becomes fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas;
this is the gate of simultaneous cultivation and realization, wherein one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the mind.

"Three times he suddenly relinquishes the consciousness of karma. Regarding the praise that says, "The light of wisdom shines universally, the consciousness of karma is suddenly relinquished, and it is dedicated toward the gate of practice," the Sūtra states:

At that time, after Mañjuśrī had exhorted the bhikṣus to resolve upon Bodhicitta, they went to the site of an ancient Buddha’s stūpa and temple to the east of the city of Vārāṇasī, where he preached the *Sūtra of the Universal Illumination of the Dharmadhātu*. At that moment, within the great ocean...

There were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nāgas who, having come to hear the Dharma, felt profound revulsion for their nāga destiny and all cast off their nāga bodies to be reborn among humans and devas.
Ten thousand nāgas attained non-retrogression from unsurpassed bodhi. This signifies that by relying on the practice of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), one awakens the mind of enlightenment;
furthermore, through the single illumination of the gateway of wisdom-light, one gives birth [to the resolve].
The consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*) was suddenly cast off at the Dead Sea; thus, when the various dragons of the great ocean came to hear the Dharma, they all abandoned their dragon bodies.

Furthermore, ten thousand dragons gave rise to the bodhicitta, signifying that by awakening one abandons karma and is thereby able to dedicate oneself toward the gateway of the ten thousand practices.
Hence, there follows the assembly of those who proceed from awakening to practice.
Regarding the fourth point, concerning the assembly that perceives the modes of conduct, the praise stating "immediately realizing the conventional as the ultimate" and so forth means:

at that time, the people of Puṇḍravardhana heard that Mañjuśrī was at the great stūpa in the Śāla Grove of the Banner of Adornment (*Vyūha-dhvaja*). Five hundred members of each of the four assemblies then left the city and went there.
Puṇḍravardhana is the City of Awakening (*Bodhi-pura*); the Banner of Adornment is the sphere of activity (*gocara*). Thus, the four assemblies left the city and arrived.

"Approaching" signifies that through awakening one proceeds toward practice. That "the fourfold assembly" consists entirely of laymen and laywomen signifies that within the mundane world one clarifies the truth.
That there are "five hundred each" signifies the perfect manifestation of the five stages. Next, regarding the praise by Sudhana:

"Relying on the treasury of merit, he reveals the fruit to manifest the cause," etc., it means that at the time of Sudhana’s birth, there were naturally occurring treasuries of the seven jewels in his home.
Five hundred precious vessels were filled with various jewels, and all his storehouses were replete with wealth and goods; for this reason, he was named Sudhana.

The *Śāstra* states: "This was brought about by the seeds of faith from previous lives, through which he experienced this birth as a reward for practicing the five stages of the path of faith in the Buddha."
Therefore, Mañjuśrī praised him, saying: "Excellent, treasury of merit! This refers to the manifestation of this hidden treasure (kośa) based upon the treasury of merit from previous lives.

It is further said that his travels to the south to visit various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) demonstrate the fruit based upon the treasury of merit, thereby manifesting the cause, initiating the practices of the five stages (pañca-sthāna), and benefiting all sentient beings.
Fifth is the assembly of those who advance through practice. This refers to the dharma-gate of Sudhana’s universal pilgrimage to the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
The number fifty represents the ten *pāramitās* for each of the five stages. The three—Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Maitreya—represent the wisdom, practice, cause, and fruit within these five stages;
they serve as the essence and function within every single dharma throughout all five stages. For further details, see [the relevant sources].
The topical outline (*ke*) further divides into six sections.

First is the "Knowledge of the Ten Abodes" (*daśavihāra-jñāna*). Regarding the praise that says, "From faith one proceeds toward concentration, meeting principle and acceding to truth," the *Śāstra* outlines this as the "Gate of Meeting Principle and Acceding to Truth through Concentration.
This is because the previously mentioned *upāsakas* and others were members of the secular world who possessed pure faith.

The boys and girls represent those whose faith is mixed with both its fundamental and derivative aspects. Furthermore, Sudhana, by relying on the seeds of faith planted in previous lives, manifests the treasury of his merit;
this serves as a general representation of the stage of faith. Here, Sudhana first beholds the Bhikṣu Meghaśrī on Mount Supārśva.

This signifies proceeding from faith toward meditative concentration (*samādhi*), thereby attaining the principle and realizing the Truth. The mountain represents the essence of concentration, and the bhikṣu...
This represents the true essence. Dechyun (Meghaśrī) is able to rain down the Dharma rain, representing supramundane beneficial conduct.

Having received Manjushri’s guidance, Sudhana ascended Mount Miao-feng and surveyed it from all sides; there he saw Dechyun walking slowly in circumambulation on a separate mountain, demonstrating that one does not abide in either meditative concentration or distraction.
This shows that after a practitioner of the Way has generated faith, they must subsequently rely upon concentration to give rise to insight (*vipaśyanā*).
When concentration and distraction are fused as a pair and the views of self and phenomena have subsided, one then accords with the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Only after the Path of Seeing can one initiate practice and enter the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśakarmapatha*). [This was taught by] the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha of the country of Samudradvāra.

1. King Prasenajit (表): This represents further observing the ocean of birth and death through contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), thereby forming a vast ocean of great wisdom that secretly brings forth benefit and profit.
2. The Bhikṣu Suvikrāntavikrāmin (三善住比丘): This represents that at this stage, the afflictions and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the three realms have been completely eliminated;

Having already prepared themselves to subdue false views and heterodox paths, these five "Elders of Liberation" (Vimokṣa-gṛhapati) and Megha are both laypersons.
This clarifies that while the three preceding bhikṣus cultivate supramundane wisdom, these two elders cultivate mundane wisdom.

Because they accord with principle and conform to truth, entering from the ultimate into the conventional, there is no obstruction between the ultimate and the conventional; this is what is called "liberation."
Sixth is the bhikṣu Sāgaradhvaja. He further symbolizes that the aforementioned two wisdoms are as vast as the ocean, crushing and destroying all the afflictions and karma of sentient beings.
Seventh is the upāsikā Śrīprabhā (here translated as Mǎnyuàn, "Fulfilling Vows"). She symbolizes entering the marketplace with compassion;
that is, fulfilling one's own original vows to universally transform sentient beings. Eighth is Vimalanetra (here translated as...)

The ninth, the Brahmin Jvalanta, signifies attaining mastery over the Dharma while appearing as a non-Buddhist, thereby causing those on false paths to subdue their afflictions (*kleśa*)—hence, he is named "Victorious" (Jvalanta).
[The Buddha] emitted heat. The maiden Daśamaitrācāriṇī was the daughter of King Siṃhadhvaja; she represented the arising of compassion from wisdom, whether amidst defilement or non-defilement.
The seventh maiden previously mentioned, although she represented great compassion, had not yet severed the habitual tendency toward the love of saving sentient beings.

At this point, the practice of great compassion is perfected; benefiting sentient beings occurs spontaneously and without further defilement or habitual tendencies. Therefore, she is symbolized by a young maiden.

Among the five stages of spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*), only the first stage directly symbolizes the specific dharma of that particular level, while the others all represent the mutual integration of wisdom and compassion.

Regarding the practice for advancement, as no specific scriptural passage has been seen, it is difficult to provide a detailed explanation. For now, I shall briefly indicate only the essential framework of the practice.

Generally speaking, before the practitioner has yet resolved their mind [upon enlightenment], fundamental wisdom is obscured by the afflictions of ignorance—both the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*).
This causes one to remain deluded and unaware, leading to a fall into the evil realms. Therefore, one must now rely upon one's own mind.
Universal Radiance Wisdom gives rise to faith; entering the Ten Abodes and acceding to the Buddha’s true wisdom is called the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).

Once true wisdom is clarified, ignorance begins to subside. However, because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still persist and the faculties are not yet matured, one employs the five stages (*pañca-avasthā*) in their repeated forward and reverse sequences to refine and grind away these tendencies, expand right view, and further cultivate merit and wisdom. This is called...

The path of cultivation: once the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are exhausted, fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) becomes perfectly round and pervasive, like the pure, vast sky free from even a trace of obscuration.
The sun of great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) shines universally upon all hidden realms; the moon of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) cools the ocean of existence.

All manifold practices and myriad virtues are fully possessed; this is called the realization of the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*). This is the ultimate path of the *Avataṃsaka* and the consummate work of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, if one seeks only the fruit of liberation and transcendence of the world, this is the narrow path of the Two Vehicles (*dvayāyāna*),

which cannot bring about the perfect realization of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Therefore, the fifty-three spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) have fully established all dharma-gates,
and Sudhana manifests his journey by traversing them all extensively, thereby inspiring practitioners to refine and cultivate themselves upon every objective condition.
Expand and broaden [the mind]; subdue the heart and endure its nature; increase that which one is incapable of; and together bring to perfection the fruit of the knowledge of all modes.
This is truly the great paradigm for the subtle completion of all things. Let practitioners take this as their model.

Next, regarding "liberation through seeing the Buddha": this is the fifth dwelling, the gateway of the Dharma taught by the spiritual friend to Sudhana, which is the entrance into the Tathāgata’s liberation of unimpeded adornment.
Within one's own body, one manifests the infinite array of adornments of all Buddha-fields;
according to one's will, one is able to see all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions. This clarifies that the conventional physical form contains [the ultimate].
This refers to the Buddha-fields. Next, regarding Śuddhipanthaka’s personal attendance upon the Buddhas: he is the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) of the seventh stage.

Because Sudhana asked about the duration and antiquity of the Dharma-gate he had attained, Śuddhipanthaka subsequently enumerated the Buddhas he had personally attended in the past, thereby clarifying the long duration of his accumulated practice.

In these, the first ten Buddhas are each assigned to the progression through the ten stages (*bhūmi*), while the final single Buddha is assigned to the eleventh stage, demonstrating that one encompasses all.

The first section concerning the twelve Buddhas is the prose portion of the sūtra that provides a general summary of Universally Saving’s causal practices. The subsequent eleven sections are the verse portion that extensively praises his personal service throughout successive kalpas.
Next is "Peaceful Ocean Served the Buddha," where the sūtra mentions that Peaceful Ocean formerly, in these ten...
Each of them attained a specific samādhi door from the Buddha. After their lives ended, they were reborn in the Sahā world.

First, they beheld the Buddhas Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa; subsequently, they beheld Vairocana Buddha and attained the liberation called "The Birth in Every Thought-Moment of the Vast and Greatly Adorned Joy. Previously, at the presence of each of these ten Buddhas, they had individually attained a samādhi.

This means that within the first bhūmi, one possesses the practices of all ten bhūmis. Subsequently, he beholds four Buddhas; this signifies his own transition from the tenth bhūmi into the eleventh bhūmi.
The remaining stages have already been included within the previous ten gates, and are therefore omitted here. Next, regarding the matter of protecting the Buddha:
when Sudhana asks how long it has been since he realized this liberation, Śubhavyūha replies that in the remote past there were [Buddhas as numerous as] atoms of dust.
When the Tathāgata appeared, his first Buddha was named Dharma-ocean Thunder-voice Radiance King (*Dharmasāgaragarjitaprabharāja*).
At that time, I was the daughter of a universal monarch and had become a bhikṣuṇī; in the presence of this Buddha, I gave rise to the bodhicitta and protected the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, there appeared in succession one hundred Buddhas, such as Vimalaprabha, whom I all approached, made offerings to, and practiced their teachings.
The fact that she is described as both a princess and a bhikṣuṇī also signifies her reliance on wisdom to cultivate both mundane and supramundane practices of compassion.
The initial mention of one Buddha followed by the mention of one hundred Buddhas likewise represents the perfect integration of the stages from the first ground onward.
This is the tenth stage. Next, regarding the "Ground of Blossoming Causes": Sudhana asked about the original aspiration that caused [the Bodhisattva] to blossom.
In response, Saṃkusumita recounted that in the past there was a Buddha named *Dharmadhātuprabhāsa-jñāna* (Wisdom Illuminating the Dharma-realm) who appeared in the world.

In that land there was a king named *Pūrṇacchattra* (Complete Canopy). During a time of calamity and disaster, the king gave rise to great compassion and brought forth all manner of things to perform a great act of giving.
At that time, when [the Buddha] was first manifesting his enlightenment, he was the daughter of a householder.

Seeing the King’s act of giving and the great benefit it brought, she made this aspiration: "May I, in the future, likewise become a place of reliance for immeasurable sentient beings shrouded in ignorance.
First, the Buddha Samantaprajña (Universal Wisdom) is mentioned; next, the account of King Paripūrṇa (Complete) and others serves to illustrate the basis of reliance.
The Universal Radiance Wisdom-Body is fully endowed with wisdom, compassion, and beneficial conduct. The rest is as explained in the annotated commentary.

Regarding the various assemblies representing the dharmas, they differ in their breadth and brevity; this is because each dharma may either contract or expand, so that people may practice them through both vertical penetration and horizontal integration without obstruction.
Next, concerning the stage of the Great Vow as the causal ground, the section heading states: "The first title clarifies the fundamental cause," and so forth.
Sudhana asked how long it had been since he first resolved his mind [on enlightenment]. Mahāpraṇidhāna replied: "In the past, during the eon of *Bhadraprabha*, ten thousand Buddhas appeared.
The first was named *Dharmacakranirghoṣapradīparāja*. At that time, there was a king named *Jayaprabha* whose kingdom was rife with the ten evils, and he consequently imposed severe punishments.
The king had a crown prince named *Suvinita*, who took pity on those suffering such torments and sought the king’s clemency."
He offered himself as a substitute for their sins, saying: "If I do not save these sentient beings, how can I save the prison of the three realms?
At that time, five hundred ministers, fearing the destruction of the state laws, requested that the prince be executed.

The Queen, with poignant grief, entreated that the prince be allowed to practice giving for half a month and cultivate merit to his heart's content before he was to face punishment. Thereupon, the charity assembly was opened.
The great assembly gathered together. At that time, the Buddha Dharmacakranirghoṣa, knowing that the time had come to discipline all sentient beings, came to preach the Dharma for them.
Thereupon, the multitude attained benefit; their suffering was extinguished and their obstacles removed.

The Crown Prince immediately taught and transformed sentient beings, causing them to give rise to roots of goodness and the gates of liberation. This clarifies the fundamental cause. At that time, the Crown Prince made a great vow.
It is so. Those five hundred ministers who sought to harm the Prince were these very five hundred people, Devadatta and his followers.
Having received the Buddha’s transformative teaching, they shall all attain Buddhahood in the future. Five hundred will appear in succession;
the first shall be named Mahākāruṇika, the second Upakārin, the third Siṃha, the fourth Trāṇa, and so on, until the last, whose name shall be...

He replied, "The physician-king refers to the sinners who were pardoned—namely, Krakucchanda and the other thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, as well as the hundreds of thousands of millions of great Bodhisattvas who, at the time of the Buddha Anantavīrya, resolved upon bodhicitta and are now, throughout the ten directions, practicing the Bodhisattva path to transform sentient beings. This clarifies their past conduct. It further states:
At that time, having saved those who were subject to punishment, I left the household life under the Buddha Wheel-Sound (Cakradhvani) and accomplished numerous Dharma-gates.
Subsequently, throughout successive lives, I encountered eighteen Buddhas, beginning with Dharmavivikta, whom I all approached and made offerings to. This clarifies the process of ascending progress.
As for the initial mention of ten thousand Buddhas appearing during the Kalpa of Good Light (Bhadrābha), it symbolizes the essence of non-effortful wisdom (*anabhoga-jñāna*).

One responds to the myriad. The Buddha’s original name was Dharmacakra-ghoṣa-gaganapradīpa-rāja (Wheel-Turning Sound-Void-Lamp King), signifying the virtuous function of generating wisdom through rectitude.
The king’s name was Jyotiṣprabha (Victorious Light), signifying the wisdom that practices compassion. His son’s name was Sudānta (Well-Subdued), signifying the conduct of compassionate wisdom.
In his kingdom, the ten non-virtues were prevalent, representing the objects to be remedied; consequently, he established severe punishments. However—

The son requested to save him. This signifies that compassion arises when good and evil manifest in contrast to one another. At that time, both the various ministers and the criminals they saved all attained the Buddha-way;
this signifies those who have achieved perfection through the transformation of wisdom and compassion. Having saved the criminals, he went to the Buddha and left the household life;
this signifies that his practice is ultimately free from defilement. Later, he encountered the Buddha in a subsequent existence; this signifies the merit of the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
This is the ultimate fruit of advancement. Indeed, relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), one responds to the myriad with the One.

The Wheel of Dharma is widely turned; the Lamp of Dharma shines far and wide. Through wisdom one practices compassion; through compassion one subdues evil, thereby bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment.
When one’s practice is ultimately untainted, the fruits of the ninth and tenth stages can be attained while sitting. Next is Wondrous Virtue (*Sudhana*).
Regarding the stage of the ground: In the distant past, there appeared a Buddha named Sovereign Banner of Merit (Vaiśravaṇaguṇadhvaja).

His mother was Queen Joyful Light (Priyaprabhā), the consort of King Jewel Flame-Eye (Ratnajvālākṣa), and at that time, Subhūti served as his wet nurse. When that Buddha was born, [the following occurred].

The devas bathed him and entrusted him to a nursing mother. Upon respectfully receiving him, the nursing mother immediately attained the Bodhisattva Samādhi of the Universal Eye, through which she saw all Buddhas of the ten directions. She also attained the Bodhisattva liberation of manifesting birth in all places;
this was its primary cause. This divine abode is in the Lumbinī Garden, where the Buddha descended to be born.
At that place, Sudhana saw her and asked, "How does one cultivate the bodhisattva practice and be born into the family of the Tathāgata?
Mañjuśrī then explained to him the ten kinds of treasuries of birth for bodhisattvas: first, the treasury of birth through the vow to always make offerings to the Buddhas;
second, the treasury of birth through the vow to generate the bodhicitta; and so on, up to the tenth, the treasury of birth through entering the stage of the Tathāgata. If...
When a Bodhisattva accomplishes these dharmas, they are born into the family of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, it says: "In the past, I made this vow:
'I vow to enter the immeasurable ocean of births of Vairocana. By the power of this vow, I am born in this garden, single-mindedly mindful of when the Bodhisattva will descend to be born.
After a hundred years had passed, the World-Honored One indeed descended. This clarifies that one enters [the womb] through various superior conditions.
Within the *ālayavijñāna*, it acts as the holy embryo of the Buddha-seed; this is called the "bodhisattva’s taking birth.
When one reaches the perfection of merit and the fulfillment of practice such that the fruit of Buddhahood manifests before one, this is called the "bodhisattva’s descent from birth.

As for the statement that "after a hundred years the World-Honored One’s fruit descends," it symbolizes that from the ninth stage (*bhūmi*) one advances to the perfect tenth stage, whereupon the fruit of Buddhahood manifests. However, this must first rely upon superior conditions to serve as the seed.
Only then can the fruit of Buddhahood be attained; therefore, it is here that the birth of the Bodhisattva is described, while on the eleventh stage, the birth of the Buddha from Māyā is recounted.
Next, regarding Gopā’s stage of practice, the first two positions symbolize those who nurture and protect through compassion.
Sudhana seeks out Gopā and arrives at the Hall of Universal Manifestation of Dharma-realm Radiance, where there is a Mistress of the Palace.
The deity of the palace is named Aśoka-guṇa (Virtue of Sorrowlessness). Accompanied by ten thousand beings, he comes to welcome Sudhana.
The Palace-Regent Deity, together with his retinue of ten thousand, represents the compassion that covers and nurtures all as the essence of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*).

His coming to welcome Sudhana signifies the harmonious convergence of the stages of practice—wherein the Great Compassion of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) is fulfilled—and the meeting within the wondrous realm of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*). Next, two positions are described.
Regarding the original cause: In the past, when Ratnapuṣpa was a king and Śākyamuni was his crown prince, Gopā was the queen consort.
At that time, she and the crown prince together beheld the Tathāgata Jayasūrya and made extensive offerings to him.
Upon hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, he immediately attained oceans of samādhis within all dharmas. He then returned to inform his father, the king, who heard this and rejoiced;
the king also went to visit the Buddha, where he heard the Dharma and gained benefit, subsequently seeking ordination.

He immediately achieved mastery over all dharma-gates and later realized the fruit of Buddhahood as Ratnakusuma. This account of the causes was related when he reached the fulfillment of the ten stages.
The Queen represents great compassion that accords with conditions; the Prince represents the wisdom of shared compassion;
the Victorious Sun represents the fruit of fundamental wisdom; and the Jewel Flower represents the fruit of subsequently attained wisdom.

Beginning with the Queen and the Prince, it thus leads to the King, the father, attaining the vision of the Victorious Sun and realizing the Jewel Flower. This clarifies that the practice of this stage consists of great compassion that accords with conditions.
In union with wisdom, one moves in accordance with the ultimate reality to initiate the subsequent realization, thereby attaining accord with the fundamental penetration as a single path.
The myriad practices of the five stages reach their ultimate mystery herein, being non-dual and without distinction. Gopā further said:
"In the past, I made offerings to the Victorious Sun (Sūryavara). After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, sixty billion nayutas of Buddhas appeared in that world."
I have served and made offerings to all these kings. The first Buddha was named Pure Body (*Vimalakāya*), and the last was named Vast Understanding (*Viśālajñāna*).
Counting these, there are fifty Buddhas; this collectively encompasses the five stages.

As for the mention of sixty billion Buddhas while citing only fifty names, it signifies that the fulfillment of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) universally includes the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) to complete the six [perfections].

These stages do not transcend the fruits of the five positions. From the initial "Victorious Sun Body" to the final "Vast Understanding," they represent the mutual fruits of the five positions, beginning with the arising of the fundamental Universal Radiance Wisdom and concluding with the Great Liberation Gate of Samantabhadra.
Essence and manifestation are mutually identical; the beginning and end are but a single thought-moment, all equally entering the Indra’s Net of Interpenetration.

The Dharma-gate of Exhaustion (*kṣayadharman*). This constitutes the ultimate stage of the tenth ground (*daśabhūmi*). The preceding section has concluded the explanation of transcending the three stages of the Sages-in-training (*tri-śaikṣa*) and entering the ten stages of the Sages (*daśārya*).

Next, the explanation begins for ascending from the ten stages of the Sages to the Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vimalā-bodhi*). First, the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyag-avabodha*).
Regarding the knowledge of the fifty-first stage, it is praised as "the wisdom manifesting at the culmination of compassion, wherein the essence of the dharma-realm is perfected.

The treatise categorizes this as the "gate of attaining Buddhahood through the arising of wisdom at the culmination of compassion. This is because prior to the tenth stage, one still relies on fundamental wisdom to nurture great compassion;
whereas in this eleventh stage, the cultivation reaches its consummation and consists purely of great compassion, which serves as the essence of the dharma-realm.
Because wisdom manifests perfectly therein, this first stage uses the Buddha’s mother, Māyā, as a symbol for the Dharma.

It demonstrates that the essence of pure compassion manifests as the Buddha of Perfect Wisdom, who benefits sentient beings according to their needs. Second is the Lord of Light, the daughter of King Samprajanya;
she symbolizes the unconditioned illuminating function of undefiled compassion within the non-conceptual wisdom of the eleventh bhūmi. Third—
The youth Samantabhadra is the teacher of the four youths skilled in the arts; this represents his pervading the ten directions as a model for the world.
The four youths skilled in the arts are able to assist in clarifying the dharma-gate of Samantabhadra; this represents the support and completion of transformation through virtue and artistry.
The virtuous and excellent laywoman Bhadrottamā [is the master of] the various medical prescriptions for the right and wrong, auspicious and inauspicious matters of the world.

He has attained mastery in all arts; he manifests peace for all beings and nourishes their lives. There is no dharma he does not understand, no practice he does not perform, and no living being he does not save.
Possessing truly vast compassion, he is therefore titled "Worthy and Victorious" (Bhadrajit). He possesses the six firm liberations.

The Elder Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin represents all meritorious practices free from attachment; by extensively cultivating merit, he remains mindful of his own non-attachment, which is called "firm liberation.
The Elder Sucandrima represents the perfection of compassion and wisdom that destroys the darkness of worldly delusion.
The Elder Ajitasena has attained the liberation of inexhaustible marks and clarifies all mental objects and states.
The collective marks of the Tathāgata represent the illusory arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*). They are able to overcome all armies of ignorance, birth-and-death, and false views.

The nine groups of Brahmins representing the tranquility of the village of the Dharma signify that within the bustling clamor of the myriad objects of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), the true stillness of the Dharma is revealed. The youth Daśakuśala and the maiden Guṇavatī represent wisdom and compassion.
They dwell in the world as a complete manifestation of illusion. They themselves say: "The two of us have realized the bodhisattva liberation of dwelling in illusion.

We clearly understand that at the end of the eleventh stage, one realizes the wisdom of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). This wisdom illuminates the mind and its objects until they are vast and free from even a speck of dust;
within the pure dharma-realm, there is only this single true wisdom. By following the function of this wisdom, all things are illusorily produced. As for the assembly in the Buddha-realm..."
All born objects rely entirely upon wisdom and abide as illusions. The nature of the myriad phenomena of the world is fundamentally detached;
not only are conditioned things like dreams and illusions in essence, but even the fruits of wisdom that arise are all abiding as illusions. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"I have attained the liberation of abiding as an illusion, seeing that all worlds are produced by the causes and conditions of abiding as illusions. All sentient beings...
All births are illusory abodes arising from the power of karma; even all bodhisattvas are illusory abodes accomplished through vows and practices.
To perceive and realize this in such a way means that ordinary beings and sages are of one essence, things and self share a common source, and all phenomena are perfectly interfused.

Dust upon dust is unobstructed; throughout the ten directions, one gazes with no object to obstruct the mind. Within this, looking back, there is no room for other things—all is abiding as an illusion.
Because it abides as an illusion and because it accords with the function of wisdom, the ocean-like functions of boundless lands are all-pervasive.
The appearances of bodies and lands throughout the ten directions mutually penetrate one another; they are neither one nor different, without beginning or end, and all-encompassing.
The dharma-realm is without coming or going; though it passes through kalpas as numerous as atoms, it is neither brief nor long.

Thus, one reaches the ultimate perfection of all the virtues and functions of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, which are perfectly interfused and sovereign—not by relying on any other method, but because of attaining the Dharma-gate of "Abiding in Illusion.
Because one realizes that all illusions are but the vanishing of reflected images, one clearly beholds the Adorned Pavilion of Maitreya.
This is the Buddha-realm Dharma-gate, which perfectly accords with the fruit-dharma.
Regarding the subsequent three stages, in each case Sudhana encounters Māyā as a result of his causal practice. As the Sūtra states:
"At that time, when Sudhana desired to see Māyā, the city-ruling goddess Ratnanetrī manifested her body in mid-air and instructed Sudhana to guard his mind."
One adorns the city of the mind, until the city of the mind becomes translucent and the city of the mind becomes richly fulfilled.
By accumulating all wholesome dharmas and eliminating all obstacles and difficulties, one then attains the vision of a spiritual friend and ultimately achieves Buddhahood.

Furthermore, there were the gods of the Lotus-Virtue Body who praised Māyā and immediately emitted immeasurable light, causing Sudhana to obtain the eye of pure radiance and forever leave behind the darkness of delusion, until he attained the all-seeing eye and beheld the appearance of all Buddhas in every land.
Moreover, there was a god who protects the Dharma Hall, who spoke from the sky, saying: "The Bodhisattva has attained..."
By means of these ten dharmas and thirteen samādhis, one attains intimacy with a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
As for the ten dharmas, they begin with the purity of mind, free from all flattery and deception, and end with the thorough discernment of all phenomena in accordance with a spiritual friend.

As for the three samādhis, they begin with the pure wheel of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) and end with the skillful knowledge that there are no faults; all of these signify entry [into the path].
This is the skillful means of the eleventh stage (*ekādaśabhūmi*). Indeed, if one can guard the city of the mind so that it becomes lucid, pure, and abundant;

and if one further attains the pure eye that sees universally, and the mind is free from flattery and deception such that one's conduct is without fault, then the practice of a Bodhisattva is complete.
Thus, one may enter the eleventh stage. Next, from the time of Siṃha Buddha downward, until...

The sutra lists many Buddhas, concluding with: "In this manner, up to and including the Tathāgata Ruci—who shall attain Buddhahood within this trichiliocosm during the Bhadrakalpa—Māyā was the mother for each of them.
As it was thus in this great trichiliocosm, so it was likewise in the oceans of immeasurable worlds. Thus, Māyā represents the ten [directions].
The first stage has as its essence the three dharmas of wisdom, principle, and great compassion, for all Buddhas are born from these three dharmas.

Regarding the latter two stages: in the past, Vairocana Tathāgata was the Universal Monarch of Great Majestic Virtue, and Māyā was the Goddess of the Site of Compassionate Virtue. At that time, the Bodhisattva Vimaladhvaja was about to attain [enlightenment].
Upon his attaining perfect enlightenment, an evil Māra arrived. The Wheel-turning King sent forth his transformed armies to protect him, whereby the Bodhisattva was able to achieve the Way.
Out of compassion, virtue, joy, and reverence for that king, he conceived the thought of him as a son. He made a vow before the Buddha, saying:
"May I always be the mother of this Wheel-turning King in every place and throughout his life until he attains Buddhahood. By these causes and conditions, [he has now become...]
She is the Mother of Buddhas. The above concludes the explanation of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). Next is the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*pratyakṣabodhi*).

Regarding the sixth assembly of those who perfectly accord with the resultant Dharma, the praise states: "Transcending the stage of fruition without interruption from the initial cause," and so forth. (10)

The first stage concludes. Devasena causes Sudhana to see Maitreya, symbolizing the transcendence of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and the realization of the fruit of Wondrous Enlightenment (*vibuddha*).
Maitreya, in turn, causes Sudhana to see Mañjuśrī again, symbolizing that upon reaching the fruit, it is identical to the cause; thus, the original and the initial are non-dual.
Therefore, although there is a vast transcendence, in reality there is no interval or distinction. At that time, Sudhana again, through Mañjuśrī, attained...
He beheld Samantabhadra and thereby fulfilled the ocean of all vows and practices of Samantabhadra, becoming equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas.
Combining these three stages constitutes the practice of the perfectly consummate fruit-dharma of all Buddhas, wherein the quiescent and active functions are eternally present;
therefore, it is categorized as "Perfectly Coinciding with the Fruit-Dharma," and is praised as "the Quiescent and Active Functions are Eternally Present. This consists of two aspects.
Within the eternal Way, one forgets cultivation and severs the realization of the Buddha-fruit; this is the eternal Way.
Now, although Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, and Samantabhadra are the names of ancient Buddhas and sages, every person is fully endowed with them. If one seeks them within oneself, what is Maitreya?
The self-nature is the fruit of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). What is Mañjuśrī? He is the essence of the universally radiant wisdom-body (*jñāna-kāya*).

What is Samantabhadra? He is the function of the wisdom of differentiated aspects. These three are fundamentally one in their essential unity, yet within the *tathāgatagarbha* of sentient beings, they manifest as diverse things according to their dispositions through the process of transformation. The Great Sage, out of compassion for them, intends to...

By governing the emotions and restoring their transformations, one relies upon the essence of the resultant Universal Radiance Wisdom (*samantaprabhā-jñāna*) which is based on Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

From this, the function of Discriminative Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) arises to establish the methods for treating habitual tendencies. When these tendencies are exhausted, wisdom becomes luminous, merit reaches its consummation, and compassion is fulfilled;
then the three wisdoms manifest perfectly and spontaneously, being fundamentally unconditioned and effortless. Therefore, they are established independently after the fifty stages.

These three demonstrate that for those who cultivate the *Avataṃsaka*, when their merit is consummated and their practice perfected, they are all able to realize these three fruits within their own nature (*svabhāva*), not obtaining them from another.
This is the true station of returning to the root and reverting to the source; it is the ultimate fruit where cultivation is forgotten and realization is transcended.
Vairocana’s bestowal of the teachings and Sudhana’s inspiration both desire that every person may reach this pinnacle.
In this regard, all practitioners should strive to reach this goal, so as not to辜负 (fail) the profound compassion of the former sages who established these teachings and inspired us.

There are other numerical categories, but they are not urgent for the purpose of representing the Dharma; fearing that they might clutter the meaning of the teaching, I shall not establish them further.

The *Commentary on the Universal Worthy’s Vows and Practices* (*Buxian Xingyuan Pin Shu*) states: "If one wishes to accomplish the inexhaustible merits of the Tathāgata, one should cultivate the ten kinds of vast vows and practices;
these include the fivefold method of repentance. The sutra says: "If one cultivates this dharma, then one will be able to..."
To bring all sentient beings to maturity, to accord with unsurpassed bodhi, and to fulfill the ocean-like conduct of Samantabhadra—these five dharmas can repent and eliminate the five obstacles;
therefore, they are called the "Five Repentances. This refers to the arising of regret and remorse; for who among men is without transgression?
Only those who have realized the wisdom of immovability can be free from fault. However, the essence of this wisdom of immovability is obstructed by the accumulation of karmic dust;
if one wishes to realize it, one must first repent and purify oneself before it can manifest clearly. Therefore, among the five practices, repentance is placed first.
When the dust is eliminated and awareness is purified, the mind and the Buddha correspond. Thus, the next practice is the invitation of all Buddhas.

They preach the Dharma to benefit sentient beings. Having relied upon the Buddha-dharma, they should be able to rejoice [in others' merit]. The benefits and blessings thus obtained should be dedicated toward enlightenment.

Because they dedicate these roots of goodness, they should give rise to great vows. This constitutes the maturing of sentient beings, the accomplishment of Bodhi, and the fulfillment of the practices of Samantabhadra;
the functional efficacy is complete, and the Buddha of Immovable Wisdom is realized from this point onward. Therefore, Samantabhadra...
The Venerable Hsing-yüan (Huiyuan) specifically established this ritual; thus, one must certainly observe and practice it until the merit of the liturgical recitation is complete.
Regarding the verse for repentance, "I contemplate the radiant crystal mirror," etc., this refers to the *Anuvyañjana-prabhāsa-parivarta*. Therein, the devaputras asked:
"How does one repent and eliminate transgressions? At that time, the Devadundubhi drum produced a sound through the power of the Bodhisattva’s samādhi.
He said: "All karmas arise from inversion; they have no fixed abode. According to what one cultivates, one receives its retribution.
It is like a crystal mirror called 'The Illuminator,' wherein boundless reflections all appear."
Yet there are no traces of coming or going. Although all karmas can produce the retributions of good and evil, they have no place from which they come or to which they go.
To know it thus is true repentance; all evils and sins are entirely purified.

The mind is luminous as original enlightenment, wondrously bright and incapable of being defiled by external objects; it is only through the deluded mind that it becomes falsely defiled. Therefore, the deluded mind—
When there is eternal cessation, all is pure. The verse of exhortation states that the Buddha is not distant from people;

it is only because people grasp at numerical categories and are deluded that they turn their backs on the Buddha themselves. If one can seek deeply, he will manifest at all times. Regarding the remaining three verses, all draw upon the intent of the sutras;
the previous commentary may be consulted for details. The formula for the Three Refuges is found in the *Zhengxing pin* (Chapter on Right Practice), fascicle 104.
